v: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him, “You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”
One of the servants of the high priest, being a relative of him whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?”
Peter therefore denied it again, and immediately the rooster crowed.
b: These are the three verses in all the Gospels
that most break the heart.
In them there are no miracles,
no discourses,
no glorious proclamations.
There is only a fire,
three questions,
and the crowing of a rooster.
John places these three verses
right in the middle of the account of Jesus’ trial.
On one side, the Lord is inside bearing witness to the truth,
on the other, a disciple is outside saying, “I am not.”
The Holy Spirit did not cover for Peter.
Because this passage is not meant to shame Peter,
it is meant to save us.
1. Failure Is a Slide, Not a Jump
At the very start of verse 25,
there is a detail that is easy to read past:
“Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself.”
Notice the words “was standing.”
This was not the first time he stood there.
Look back at verse 18:
the servants and officers had made a fire of coals because it was cold,
and Peter was standing with them, warming himself.
In other words,
after the first time he denied the Lord,
Peter did not leave.
He was still standing in the same spot.
He was still warming himself at the same fire.
This is the most important sentence in the whole passage.
After the first denial,
Peter did not leave that fire,
and so there was a second time,
and a third time.
Dear family,
we often think failure is a decision made in a single moment.
As if a person were standing at the edge of a cliff
and suddenly leaped.
It is not so.
Failure almost never happens by jumping.
Failure happens by sliding.
Inch by inch,
slipping downward without noticing.
I think of a picture.
A car is parked on a slope.
No one pushes it.
No one touches it.
As long as the handbrake is not set tight,
it will begin to move on its own.
At first it moves extremely slowly,
so slowly that the person sitting in it cannot feel it at all.
By the time he notices,
the car has already slid to the bottom of the hill.
Peter was that car.
He did not decide to deny the Lord three times.
He simply—did not leave the fire.
That fire was warm.
That courtyard had a roof.
Outside it was cold,
and he still wanted to see what would happen to the Lord.
His motives were not even bad.
But he was standing in the wrong place.
So remember this sentence:
where you stay after you fall
decides whether you will fall again.
We are not defeated by the first weakness.
We are defeated because after the first weakness,
we could not bear to leave.
That group chat that made you speak out of turn the first time,
that relationship that stirred your heart the first time,
that setting where you compromised the first time,
that position where you lied the first time—
if after you fall you are still standing there warming yourself,
the second time will surely come.
Paul said:
“Let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.”
(1 Corinthians 10:12)
Careful about what?
Not only careful about your heart,
but careful about your feet.
Be careful where you stand.
Brothers and sisters,
if a place comes to your mind today,
a place you know you should not stay in any longer,
that is not an accusation.
That is the Holy Spirit’s gentle hand
tugging at your sleeve.
2. He Did Not Fail to Love the Lord, He Was Afraid
Verse 27 is only one sentence:
“Peter therefore denied it again.”
The word “again” is heavy.
It tells us
this was not a slip.
This was a repetition.
But I want to pause here
and say a fair word for Peter,
and a fair word for ourselves as well.
Why was Peter there?
Because the other disciples had all run away.
Eleven men scattered and fled,
and only he followed into the courtyard of the high priest.
He had even drawn a sword in the garden and struck a man.
A man who does not love the Lord
does not draw a sword.
A man who does not love the Lord
does not follow all the way there.
So Peter’s problem
was never that “he did not love the Lord.”
Peter’s problem was—
he was afraid.
Verse 26 makes it very clear:
the one who asked him
was a relative of the man whose ear he had cut off.
That was not a casual question.
That was a pair of eyes that recognized him.
The meaning of those words was almost:
“You’re the one who swung the sword.”
At that moment Peter
smelled danger.
His love was real,
and his fear was real too.
Dear family,
we need to say one thing very honestly:
love and fear
can exist inside the same person at the same time.
A person who truly loves the Lord
may, in some setting,
quietly set his faith down.
It is a very light movement.
So light that others cannot see it.
At a table with colleagues,
when everyone starts mocking people who believe in Jesus,
you laugh a little
and say nothing.
In front of a client,
you know that matter is not in line with the truth,
but you just “go along with the process.”
At a gathering of relatives,
someone asks, “Are you still going to church?”
You say, “It’s okay, I go once in a while.”
At that moment,
you did not curse the Lord,
you did not abandon the faith.
You just—
took off that robe,
gently,
and laid it on the chair.
What Peter said was not anything fierce either.
He said only two words:
“I am not.”
Very short.
Very light.
Yet three times.
I say these things
not so that we would condemn ourselves.
If after reading this passage
you feel only shame,
then we have read it wrong.
Because the Bible records Peter’s failure
not so that we would see “how bad Peter was,”
but so that we would see:
the Lord knew all along,
and He still chose him,
still prayed for him,
still came back to find him after the resurrection.
A person the Lord can use
is not someone who has never said “I am not.”
He is someone who, after saying “I am not,”
is still willing to turn back.
3. Immediately the Rooster Crowed
The second half of verse 27:
“Immediately the rooster crowed.”
The word “immediately”
is written with great power.
Not a day later.
Not an hour later.
It was the very instant that “I am not” hit the ground.
In Roman reckoning of time,
the watch between midnight and dawn
was called “the rooster’s crowing.”
That is the darkest hour of the day.
The night had not yet passed,
but the rooster was already crowing.
Dear family,
let me tell you something:
that crow of the rooster
was not punishment.
That crow of the rooster was grace.
Think about it.
If God had done nothing,
what would have happened?
Peter would have had a fourth time.
A fifth time.
He would have slid all the way down,
to a place from which he could never return.
But God did not let him sink all the way.
God used a sound
to wake him up.
A rooster.
The most ordinary,
least spiritual sound,
one that happens every morning.
God used it,
in the darkest moment,
to pull a sinking disciple back up.
I think of the smoke alarm at home.
It always goes off in the middle of the night.
The sound is piercing,
annoying,
and our first reaction is often:
“Somebody go turn that thing off!”
But we all know
it is not trying to bother you.
It is trying to save you.
It sounds
because it smelled the smoke before you did.
That crow of the rooster
was the alarm God placed in Peter’s life.
Piercing,
humiliating,
yet loving.
And the Gospel of Luke records an even deeper stroke.
At the very moment the rooster crowed,
the Lord turned
and looked at Peter.
The Lord was on trial at that time.
He Himself was falsely accused,
mocked,
spat upon.
In such circumstances,
He still turned
and looked at the disciple who had just denied Him.
Family,
please do not think of that look as a glare.
There was no condemnation in that look.
That look was heartache.
It was, “I knew you would do this, I told you so,
and I have already been praying for you.”
When Peter saw that look,
he went out and wept bitterly.
Weeping bitterly is not a sign of destruction.
Weeping bitterly is the beginning of turning back.
What is truly frightening
is never the weeping.
It is hearing the rooster crow
and feeling nothing in your heart.
God often wakes us up like this today too.
Sometimes it is a sentence in a sermon
that suddenly seems to be spoken just for you.
Sometimes it is a passage of Scripture you open at random,
and every word pierces your heart.
Sometimes it is a sudden quiet,
lying awake at night,
when a voice in your heart asks you:
“Where have you been walking lately?”
That is not a coincidence.
That is the rooster’s crow.
That is the Lord turning to look at you.
4. The Root of Failure Is “Self”; the Root of Hope Is the Lord’s Intercession
We must ask one last question:
How did Peter come to this point?
The answer lies a few hours earlier.
In the upper room,
Peter had beaten his chest and said:
“Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”
(Matthew 26:35)
Listen to where the weight of that sentence falls.
I cannot.
I surely will not.
I can certainly do it.
Peter’s failure
did not begin at the fire in the courtyard.
It began with that sentence, “I can certainly do it.”
This is exactly what the 321 principles say again and again:
having self is the root of humanity’s fall,
and pride is the root of the problem.
Pride is not always looking down on others.
The most common pride
is “I think I can stand on my own.”
Peter was not a bad man.
Peter was a self-confident man.
And self-confidence and faith
differ by only one word,
yet their directions are completely opposite.
Faith puts the weight on the Lord.
Self-confidence puts the weight on oneself.
Whatever sets out from “I can certainly do it”
will in the end fall.
Because that load-bearing pillar
was never able to hold up.
The one who truly stands
sets out from a different sentence:
“I cannot, but the Lord can.”
Humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place.
Letting man be man and God be God.
Humility overcomes pride,
self-denial overcomes Satan.
But family,
today’s message cannot stop here.
Because long before Peter fell,
the Lord had already prepared his way out.
The Lord said to him:
“I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail.”
Listen carefully to this sentence.
The Lord did not say:
I prayed for you, that you would not fall.
What the Lord said was:
that your faith would not fail.
The falling,
the Lord did not prevent.
The failing of faith,
the Lord prayed against.
Because the Lord knew
that what is truly fatal is not that one fall,
but not getting up after falling.
So Peter’s story
did not stop at the rooster’s crow.
The Gospel of John records a most beautiful ending.
In chapter 18,
there was a fire of coals,
where Peter said “I am not” three times.
By chapter 21,
the risen Lord, by the Sea of Galilee,
made another fire of coals.
In the whole Gospel of John,
the word “fire of coals” appears only these two times.
The Lord did this on purpose.
He brought Peter back to the same scene,
back to the same smell,
and then asked him three times:
“Do you love me?”
Three denials,
three restorations.
The Lord did not dig up the old accounts.
The Lord took the old accounts
and healed them one by one.
Family,
this is our hope.
Falling is not the end.
Refusing to come back is.
If today there is a fire in your heart,
where you once said “I am not,”
please believe:
the Lord is already there,
and has made another fire of coals for you.
He is not waiting to interrogate you.
He is waiting to ask you one thing:
“Do you love me?”
The Light of the 321 Principles—Turning Defeat into Victory, Becoming an Overcomer
Today’s passage
reveals the weightiest path in the 321 principles.
An overcomer is not someone who has never been defeated.
An overcomer
is someone who turns defeat into victory.
Peter here is a complete failure.
Not a small weakness,
but three public denials.
Yet fifty days later,
at Pentecost,
the one who stood up and preached to the whole city of Jerusalem
was this same Peter.
The same mouth.
First it said “I am not,”
later it said, “This Jesus whom you crucified,
God has made both Lord and Christ.”
What happened in between?
What happened in between
was the death of a “self.”
That boastful Peter died.
That Peter who said “I can certainly do it” died.
The one who came alive
was a Peter who knew he could fall,
and therefore held on to the Lord with all his might.
This is the life of the old self, full of self,
becoming the life of the new self, emptied of self.
Being emptied of self is not nothingness,
being emptied of self is entering the limitless.
What Peter lost
was that small “me”
that held itself up by its own strength.
What Peter gained
was a vessel filled with the Holy Spirit,
one the Lord could use as He pleased.
And the calling the Lord gave Peter
is also the heart of 321:
“When once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”
Those who have fallen
know best how to help others up.
Those who have been restored
are the least likely to judge others.
So the Lord wants not only that we ourselves overcome,
the Lord wants us to walk alongside every person,
so that together we become overcomers.
If you are at the bottom of the hill today,
remember:
the Lord has already prayed for you.
If you have already turned back today,
please go and find the one still standing by the fire.
Gently,
without blame,
bring him back.
The Response of Life
This passage reminds us:
First, failure is a slide, not a jump. Where you stay after you fall decides whether you will fall again.
Second, love and fear can exist in the same person. It is not that we do not love the Lord; we are simply too afraid in certain settings.
Third, the crow of the rooster is grace, not punishment. God does not let us sink all the way down; He always wakes us up with a sound.
Fourth, whatever sets out from “I can certainly do it” will fall. The one who truly stands sets out from “I cannot, but the Lord can.”
Fifth, falling is not the end; refusing to come back is. The Lord has already prayed for us, and has already made a fire of coals on the shore, waiting for us.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we come before You, thinking of Peter, and thinking of ourselves. Lord, we confess that we too have stood beside that fire, gently set You down, and said, “I am not.” It is not that we do not love You; we were only afraid. Have mercy on us, and remove from within us that boastful “self,” so that we no longer set out from “I can certainly do it,” but from “I cannot, but the Lord can.” Give us a sensitive heart, so that when Your rooster crows, we hear it at once, turn back at once, and slide down no further. Lord Jesus, thank You that even while on trial You turned and looked at Peter; there was no condemnation in that look, only heartache; look at us like that today too. Thank You that You have already prayed for us, that our faith would not fail. Turn our defeat into victory, make us Your overcomers, and with the same gentleness let us walk alongside every person near us who has fallen, that together we may overcome. May all the glory be to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. In your life, is there a “place beside the fire” you should have left long ago but keep being unwilling to leave? Are you willing to get up and walk away today?
2\. What “rooster’s crow” has God used lately to remind you: a word, a Scripture passage, or a sudden silence? Did you turn back then, or did you shut it off?

v: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
Pilate therefore went out to them, and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.”
Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.” Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is illegal for us to put anyone to death,”
that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
b: It was not yet fully light.
A crowd was leading Jesus,
from the courtyard of the high priest
to the headquarters of the Roman governor.
They stopped outside the door.
They would not go in.
Because entering a Gentile’s house,
by their rules,
would make them defiled,
and they could not eat the Passover meal that evening.
Brothers and sisters,
please keep this scene in your heart.
A crowd standing outside the threshold,
carefully making sure their shoes did not step inside,
while in their hands they held an innocent man,
about to send Him to be crucified.
These five verses
do not give any grand teaching.
They simply set a picture before us.
And this picture
is more alarming than any rebuke.
1. They Feared Defilement, but Not Shedding Innocent Blood
Verse 28 says:
“They themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.”
This is the most glaring sentence in the whole passage.
The same people,
on the same morning,
did two things at once.
One was:
refusing to cross a threshold,
so as not to be ceremonially unclean.
The other was:
with their own hands handing the Son of God
over to the Romans to be put to death.
They were extremely sensitive about the first thing.
About the second thing,
they felt nothing at all.
It was not that they did not know the law.
They knew it better than anyone.
What kind of contact makes one unclean,
how long until one is clean again,
what water to wash with,
they had it all memorized perfectly.
But the clearest commands in the law:
“You shall not murder.”
“You shall not give false testimony to frame someone.”
These two,
they were breaking together that very morning.
They could keep the ritual,
but could not keep a clean conscience.
The rules of purity could be kept down to the last detail,
while the intent to kill in their hearts went entirely unnoticed.
How terrible this is.
A person can get every detail right on the outside,
while inside he is completely warped,
and does not know it at all.
Because they had a ruler.
But that ruler
measured only the outside.
The Bible says:
“Yahweh sees not as man sees: for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
(1 Samuel 16:7)
That day,
they measured very accurately.
But God was looking somewhere else.
2. Mistaking “Outward Cleanness” for “Inward Cleanness” Is Religion’s Most Dangerous Disease
This verse
is not a problem unique to the Jews.
It is the disease
that religion has caught most easily from ancient times until now.
Because outward cleanness
can be seen.
Inward cleanness
cannot be seen.
What can be seen
is easy to do
and easy to be praised for.
What cannot be seen
has no one watching,
and no one applauding.
So people slowly
put all their effort into what can be seen,
and after a while,
they truly think that is everything.
The Lord Jesus said this very directly long ago.
He said:
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness.”
(Matthew 23:25)
The outside of the cup is polished until it shines.
Set on the table, it looks beautiful.
But inside it is dirty.
A person who wipes only the outside
is not deceiving others;
he is mostly deceiving himself.
Here I would like to share an illustration with you.
There is a car,
and its owner treasures it greatly.
Every weekend he takes it to be washed,
waxed,
vacuumed,
the wheel rims scrubbed bright.
Parked by the roadside,
everyone turns to look.
But the hood,
he has never opened.
The oil inside has long since gone bad,
the radiator is leaking,
the belt is already cracked.
The outside gets shinier every year.
The inside gets worse every year.
One day on the highway,
the car smoked and stopped.
He felt wronged:
“But I wash my car every single week!”
Brothers and sisters,
a car wash cannot replace an oil change.
Maintenance on the outside
can never save the engine on the inside.
The people standing at the door of the headquarters that day
were exactly the ones who had washed the car cleanest.
3. This Mirror Is Meant to Show Us Ourselves
When we get to this point,
it is very easy to do one thing:
shake our heads
and say:
“These Pharisees were truly terrible.”
And then close the Bible.
But the Bible records this passage
not so that we would scold people of the past.
It is so that we would look in the mirror.
So now,
let us gently place this passage
back upon ourselves.
We too might:
attend every gathering,
never miss an offering,
pray at set times,
never be late to small group,
and put our hands to serving.
From the outside,
nothing is lacking.
But in our hearts toward a certain person,
we have never been willing to forgive.
Thinking of him makes us uncomfortable.
We don’t mention it in front of the brothers and sisters,
but the wall in our heart has never been torn down.
Perhaps it has been five years.
Perhaps ten years.
Outwardly we entered the temple,
inwardly we did not go in.
I also think of another picture.
There is a wall,
and because a water pipe inside is leaking,
a patch of damp rot has grown in the corner.
The owner does not like how it looks,
so he buys paint
and brushes on a coat.
Three months later it shows up again,
so he brushes on another coat.
After seven or eight coats,
the wall gets thicker and thicker,
and the problem gets bigger and bigger.
Because what that wall truly needs
is not paint.
It needs the wall opened up
and the pipe inside replaced.
Many of us
keep painting over our own lives.
Try a little harder.
Hold out a little longer.
Read one more chapter of the Bible.
None of these are bad things.
But if the pipe inside is not replaced,
no matter how many coats go on the outside,
it will still seep through.
The Lord Jesus said:
“There is nothing from outside of the man, that going into him can defile him; but the things which proceed out of the man are those that defile the man.”
(Mark 7:15)
The real problem
has never been on this side or that side of the threshold.
It is in the heart.
4. “We Have No Authority to Put Anyone to Death”—Man Thinks He Is Shifting Blame, but God Is Fulfilling His Plan
Verse 31,
Pilate said something very interesting:
“Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.”
Pilate did not want to take this case.
He could see it was a religious dispute.
He wanted to kick the ball back.
How did the Jews answer?
“It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”
At that time, this was the fact.
Under Roman rule,
the authority for the death penalty was held by the governor.
But these words
were also words of evasion.
The meaning was:
the one to do it is not us,
it is you.
We are only bringing the man.
The blood will not be on our hands.
They thought they were shedding responsibility.
But verse 32 says something startling:
“that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.”
So it turns out
that this evasion of theirs
pushed the whole matter
onto the track God had already set.
Because under Jewish law,
a blasphemer is put to death by stoning.
But Jesus Himself had said:
“I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
The Bible goes on to explain:
“But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.”
Lifted up.
That is the cross.
That is a Roman punishment,
not the Jewish way.
So,
Jesus had to die on a Roman cross.
Not under a pile of stones outside the city.
And that morning,
what brought this about
was, of all things, a sentence shifting responsibility.
Brothers and sisters,
please see this clearly.
Man thinks he is dodging.
God is fulfilling.
Man thinks he is scheming.
God is paving the road.
Man thinks he himself closed that door,
but in fact that door
was the other door God was opening.
5. It Looks as if Man Is in Control, but from Beginning to End God Is in Control
Let us look at the whole scene once more.
The priests are mobilizing.
Pilate is questioning.
The crowd is clamoring.
It is not yet light,
yet the noise of voices is already boiling.
It looks as if
the initiative is entirely in human hands.
And Jesus?
He is bound.
He is led along.
He is pushed back and forth.
He looks like the one with the least power.
But verse 32 says, quietly, one sentence:
“that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.”
With one sentence,
the sovereignty of the whole picture
is turned around.
It turns out the priests’ scheming,
Pilate’s evasion,
the crowd’s shouting,
not one of them stepped outside God’s plan.
The apostle Peter later said very clearly on the day of Pentecost:
“him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed.”
(Acts 2:23)
On one side, “the hand of lawless men.”
On the other, “the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God.”
Two phrases placed in the same verse.
Man must bear his own responsibility.
God is also accomplishing His will.
Dear family,
this is a great comfort for us today.
You may be standing today in a scene
where it looks as if others are deciding everything.
The decision is in your supervisor’s hands.
The decision is in the other party’s hands.
The decision is in the hands of the system,
of time,
of circumstances.
You are like the one being led along,
unable to get in a single word.
Please remember this verse.
On that morning,
Jesus seemed to have the least sovereignty,
yet from beginning to end,
what drove the whole matter
was the plan of heaven.
Not a meeting on earth.
The Light of the 321 Principles—Change Your Concepts and Your Life Changes, Change Your Life and Your Living Changes
Today’s passage
shines a very bright light on one of the main threads of the 321 principles.
We often say:
change your concepts, and your life changes.
Change your life, and your living changes.
We also often speak of
the five layers of change, from the inside out—
concepts,
life,
living,
relationships,
ministry.
Please notice the order of these five layers.
It is from the inside out.
Not from the outside in.
The people standing outside the headquarters that day
were walking in exactly the opposite direction.
They began changing from the outermost.
They fixed ministry—
the feast was properly arranged.
They fixed living—
the rules were strictly kept.
They fixed relationships—
in front of people they called one another Rabbi.
But the two innermost layers,
concepts and life,
had never been touched.
Their concepts had not changed,
so when they saw the Son of God,
they did not recognize Him.
Their life had not changed,
so they could keep purity with one hand
while condemning an innocent man with the other.
The more beautifully the outer three layers were done,
the less visible the breach in the inner two layers became.
This is why
true change must begin from within.
Not from outward religious behavior.
\*\*Outward behavior can change quickly, but inner concepts must be turned over by the Holy Spirit layer by layer.\*\*
So what we ask for
is not more rules.
It is a new pair of eyes.
From man’s viewpoint,
to God’s viewpoint.
From looking at the outward appearance,
to looking at the heart.
When the concept changes,
life follows.
When life changes,
living naturally changes.
When living changes,
relationships can truly be restored.
When relationships are right,
ministry is alive.
This order cannot be reversed.
Once it is reversed,
we become that crowd:
standing in neat rows outside the threshold,
while in our hearts we stand across from God.
David’s prayer in the Psalms
is exactly the starting point of this path:
“Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts.”
(Psalm 51:6)
What God wants
was never the clean shoes outside the threshold.
It is the true heart inside the threshold.
The Response of Life
This passage reminds us:
First, outward cleanness is not inward cleanness. Keeping the ritual does not necessarily mean keeping a clean conscience; this is something every one of us must watch out for.
Second, the greatest danger of religion is not being able to see oneself. Because the outside is all done right, we assume there is no problem inside.

Third, this mirror is meant to show ourselves, not others. Attending every gathering and never missing an offering, yet harboring someone in our heart we refuse to forgive—that is entering the temple outwardly while not entering inwardly.

Fourth, man thinks he is shifting blame, but God is fulfilling His plan. A single sentence, “We have no authority to put anyone to death,” actually fulfilled the prophecy that the Lord would be lifted up.
Fifth, it looks as if man is in control, but from beginning to end God is in control. The scene in which you stand today is also within His plan.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for placing a mirror before us through today’s passage. Lord, we see that crowd standing outside the headquarters, afraid of being defiled, yet not afraid to send Your Son to be crucified; as we are alarmed, we also know that it is not only them, it could also be us. Shine Your light within us. Wherever we have done well on the outside but have long since gone cold on the inside, please point it out; wherever we have kept covering over with paint and never opened up to repair, please begin Your work. Lord, we do not want to polish only the outside of the cup; we ask You to cleanse the inside of the cup. First change our concepts, then change our life, and then change our living, our relationships, our ministry, so that all of it comes from the inside out, truly flowing from the heart. And cause us, in situations where we seem powerless, still to believe that Your hand is always in control. May Jesus be King within us, and may all the glory be Yours. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. In my life of faith, is there something “neatly done on the outside, but long gone cold on the inside”? Today, what spot am I willing to let God touch first?
2\. Is there still someone in my heart whom I have not forgiven to this day? If true change comes from the inside out, what is the first step I can take today?

v: Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?”
Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”

Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
b: This is a most unusual conversation.
On one side is the governor of the Roman Empire,
holding the power of life and death.
On the other is a bound prisoner,
who has not slept all night,
who was sold,
seized,
and rejected by men.
By the world’s way of seeing,
the outcome of this trial
was already written in who held the power.
But if you read these five verses closely,
you will discover something wonderful:
the one asking becomes more and more flustered,
while the one being asked remains calm throughout.
Because in this headquarters,
the one truly seated on the judgment seat
is not Pilate.
1. The Bound Prisoner Is the True King in This Headquarters
Verse 33,
Pilate called Jesus into the headquarters
and asked Him:
“Are you the King of the Jews?”
We must first understand the situation at that time.
When the Jews brought Jesus before Pilate,
the charge they used was political.
They knew that
a religious accusation like “blasphemy”
meant nothing to the Romans.
But “claiming to be a king” was different.
In the Roman Empire,
there was only one king.
Anyone who set himself up as king
was committing treason.
So Pilate asked this very question the moment he opened his mouth.
He wanted to confirm:
could this man before him
be a threat to Caesar?
But look at Jesus’ response:
no defending Himself,
no pleading,
no clearing Himself of guilt.
Instead, He asked a question.
A bound man,
asking a question before the governor.
Dear family,
please see this picture clearly.
On the surface,
Pilate is questioning Jesus.
In truth,
Jesus is questioning Pilate.
Pilate had military power in his hands,
the official seal,
the authority to crucify,
yet he stood before the truth
and could not stand on a single word.
Jesus had nothing in His hands,
not even freedom,
yet within Him was a kingdom.
This is what the Bible keeps letting us see:
true authority
is not in whose hands it is held,
but in who dwells within whom.
2. “Do You Say This of Yourself?”—Faith Cannot Forever Depend on Other People’s Answers
Verse 34,
the Lord asked a question of great weight:
“Do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
These words
deserve to be chewed over again and again.
Jesus was not stalling for time.
He was saying to Pilate:
you ask me whether I am a king;
are you asking on behalf of the chief priests,
or do you yourself want to know in your own heart?
Are you handling an official matter,
or facing a person?
What matters most
has never been the correct answer in our mouths,
but the true attitude in our hearts.
Pilate’s answer was very honest,
and very regrettable.
In verse 35 he said:
“Am I a Jew?”
The meaning was:
this is your Jewish affair,
and has nothing to do with me.
I am only handling the case according to procedure.
How many people stop right here for their whole lives.
They have heard the name of Jesus.
They have heard others’ testimonies.
They have heard a great deal from parents,
from friends,
from pastors.
But not once
have they stood before the Lord and answered for themselves.
Dear family,
there is one thing
no one can do for us.
Someone else’s faith cannot save me.
Someone else’s experience cannot be counted as mine.
My mother loving the Lord very much
does not mean I know the Lord.
Having spent thirty years in the church
does not mean I have personally had one real encounter with the Lord.
One day we will stand before the Lord,
and the Lord will not ask:
“What does your church say about me?”
He will ask:
“Who do you say that I am?”
The 321 principles say:
the first step in changing concepts is information,
but information is not revelation.
Hearing
is only information.
When the heart is opened
and you recognize it for yourself,
that is revelation.
From information to revelation,
from other people’s words to your own conviction,
faith truly begins.
3. “My Kingdom Is Not of This World”—Different in Source, Different in Nature, Different in Method
Verse 36,
the Lord spoke the most pivotal sentence of the whole passage:
“My Kingdom is not of this world.”
These words are easily misunderstood.
The Lord was not saying:
my kingdom does not operate in this world.
He was not saying:
my kingdom is only in heaven,
and has nothing to do with life on earth.
The Lord meant:
the source,
the nature,
and the method of my kingdom
do not come from this world.
Let us see how He explained it Himself.
“If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews.”
Notice,
the Lord did not say He had no servants.
He did.
In the garden of Gethsemane He had said
that He could ask the Father to send more than twelve legions of angels.
It was not that He had no power.
It was that He did not use that kind of power.
Kingdoms of the world
expand by force,
are maintained by fighting,
and make people bow by might.
The Kingdom of God
by the cross,
by self-denial,
wins people’s hearts through truth.
Kingdoms of the world can occupy a piece of land,
but cannot occupy a heart.
The Kingdom of God occupies no land,
yet enters the deepest part of the human heart.
This is also why
the Roman Empire has long since become history,
while the Lord’s Kingdom has kept expanding for two thousand years.
Here is a very sober reminder.
If the church uses the world’s methods to build God’s Kingdom,
what is built
will not be God’s Kingdom.
Using comparison,
using competition,
using large crowds and strong momentum,
using power to overpower others—
that is the way of the kingdoms of the world.
The 321 principles say it clearly:
the one purpose
is to build God’s system.
God’s system has God’s methods.
Not seizing power,
but laying down power and returning to one’s place.
Not displaying ourselves,
but letting Jesus receive all the glory.
Pride is leaving one’s place and seizing power,
wanting to take God’s place.
Humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place,
letting man be man
and God be God.
That day Pilate wanted to seize power,
and as a result his name was written into the Apostles’ Creed,
as the one who crucified the Lord.
That day Jesus laid down power,
and as a result He became King of kings.
4. “For This Reason I Was Born, and for This Reason I Have Come into the World”—A Life’s Purpose as Clear as a Straight Line
Verse 37,
Pilate asked again:
“Are you a king then?”
Jesus answered:
“You say that I am a king. For this reason I was born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth.”
I love the words “for this reason I was born.”
The purpose of the Lord’s whole life
was as clear as a straight line.
From the manger to the cross,
not once did He deviate.
He knew where He came from.
He knew where He was going.
He knew why He was here.
So even bound in the headquarters,
His direction was not confused.
Now look at ourselves in turn.
We are busy.
Schedules full.
Work never finished.
But if someone asked you tonight:
“What are you living for?”
many of us would be stunned.
We can say what we are busy with,
but cannot say what we are living for.
It is like a person who gets into the driver’s seat,
starts the engine,
presses the accelerator hard,
and drives very fast,
but has never entered a destination.
The faster he goes,
the farther he only takes himself to get lost.
Dear family,
the problem of life has never been speed,
it is direction.
And the problem of direction
is really a problem of lordship.
Whoever sits in the driver’s seat
decides where to go.
I can confess with my mouth that Jesus is Lord,
yet never be willing to give up the steering wheel.
I can ask the Lord to sit beside me and give directions,
yet insist on driving myself.
That is not called letting Jesus be King,
that is called asking Jesus to be a consultant.
The first of the two cores of the 321 principles is:
let Jesus be King.
Letting Him be King
is not doing a few more spiritual things,
it is handing over the driver’s seat.
Once He is King,
my whole life has a straight line.
5. “Everyone Who Is of the Truth Listens to My Voice”—Hearing Is a Question of Whom the Heart Belongs To
The last sentence of verse 37:
“Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
The Lord did not say:
everyone with sharp ears listens to my voice.
He did not say:
everyone who has read many books listens to my voice.
He said:
everyone who is of the truth.
The word “of”
speaks of belonging,
of ownership,
of whose this person ultimately is.
Pilate that day heard the Lord’s voice with his own ears,
face to face,
only a few steps away.
He even asked:
“What is truth?”
And after asking, he turned and went out.
He heard the sound,
but did not hear the words.
It is like a radio.
There are always radio waves in the air.
The program is always broadcasting.
Whether you hear it
does not depend on how high the volume is turned,
but on whether the frequency is tuned in.
If the frequency is wrong,
no matter how loud, it is only noise.
Once the frequency is right,
even the faintest sound is perfectly clear.
Inside us there is also a frequency.
That frequency
is whom our heart really belongs to.
If the heart belongs to self,
the Lord’s words coming in become a harsh demand.
If the heart belongs to the world,
the Lord’s words coming in seem out of place.
If the heart belongs to the truth,
the moment the Lord speaks,
something inside us immediately recognizes:
this is my Master’s voice.
So,
when we feel that God seems not to be speaking,
the problem is often not on God’s side.
It is not that He has fallen silent,
it is that our frequency has switched channels.
The 321 principles say:
the third of the three foundations
is that the Holy Spirit is my guide.
The Holy Spirit’s guidance is never lacking,
what is lacking is a heart tuned to the right frequency.
Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit,
do not use the head and rely on yourself.
When we use the head,
we hear only our own analysis.
When we use the heart,
we can hear the Lord’s voice.
The Light of the 321 Principles—Let Jesus Be King, Starting with This One Heart of Mine
Today’s passage
from beginning to end speaks of only one thing:
kingship.
Who is King.
Pilate thought Caesar was king.
The chief priests thought they themselves were king.
The crowd thought whoever was loudest was king.
And the One who is truly King,
bound,
standing among them,
quietly said:
“My Kingdom is not of this world.”
The first of the two cores of the 321 principles
is letting Jesus be King.
But we must ask a very practical question:
where does He reign as King?
The answer is:
first in this one heart of mine.
God’s Kingdom does not first come down upon systems,
does not first come down upon organizations,
it first comes down in the human heart.
The Lord’s Prayer says:
“Your Kingdom come,
Your will be done on earth
as it is in heaven.”
How will His Kingdom come on earth?
Through people who hand over their hearts, one by one.
When one person lets the Lord be King,
that person has within him a small piece of the land of the Kingdom of Heaven.
When one family lets the Lord be King,
that family becomes the Kingdom of Heaven on earth.
When a group of people let the Lord be King,
God’s system is established.
This is our one purpose:
to build God’s system,
to fulfill the Lord’s Prayer.
So the question we most need to ask ourselves today
is not “why is the world such a mess,”
but:
\*\*Right now, who is reigning as king inside me?\*\*
Is it my emotions that reign as king?
Is it my pride that reigns as king?
Is it my plans,
my grievances,
my fears that reign as king?
Or is it the Lord who was born for this,
who came into the world for this,
who died and rose again for me,
truly seated on the throne of my heart?
The Response of Life
This passage reminds us:
First, true authority is not in whose hands it is held, but in who dwells within. The bound Lord was the true King in that headquarters.
Second, faith cannot forever depend on other people’s answers. The Lord will personally ask me one thing: Do you say this of yourself?
Third, God’s Kingdom has God’s methods. Not by fighting and might, but by the cross, self-denial, and truth.
Fourth, a life needs a clear purpose. The Lord was born for this; I also need to know what I am living for.
Fifth, hearing the Lord’s voice is a question of whom the heart belongs to. It is not a problem of the ears, it is a problem of frequency.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see today a picture we will never forget: our Lord standing bound before the governor, yet the true King of the whole universe. Lord, forgive us for often being like Pilate, knowing You only through what others say, and never having stood before You to answer for ourselves. Ask us Yourself today: Do you say this of yourself? And give us courage to answer with our own mouths: Lord, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Remove from within us every thought of building by the world’s methods, and make us willing to walk the way of the cross, of self-denial, and of truth. Tune the frequency within our hearts, that we may become people who are of the truth, who recognize Your voice the moment we hear it, and obey the moment we recognize it. May Your Kingdom come, may Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven; may You reign as King today in this one heart of mine, that I may live my whole life for this, and give all the glory to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. If the Lord asked you in person today, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others tell you about me?” how would you answer? How much of your knowledge of Jesus is from your own personal experience?

2\. In a matter you are handling right now, are you letting the Lord sit in the driver’s seat, or only inviting Him to sit beside you as a consultant? Which steering wheel can you hand back to Him today?

v: Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.
But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
b: This is the shortest
and most heartbreaking conversation
in the whole Bible.
Jesus had just said:
“Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
Pilate answered with one line:
“What is truth?”
And then
he turned and walked away.
Within these few short verses,
there is a man who asked a question but would not wait for the answer,
a governor who found no guilt in Him and yet condemned Him,
and a crowd who would rather have a robber
than a Savior.
And the One standing in the middle
did not say a single extra word.
He was walking toward our cross.
1. He Asked About Truth, but Would Not Wait for the Answer
At the beginning of verse 38,
Pilate said:
“What is truth?”
This sentence
may be the most famous question in human history.
For two thousand years it has been quoted by countless philosophers,
thinkers,
and writers.
But we need to notice something.
The Bible goes on:
“When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews.”
He asked,
and then he left.
He did not wait for an answer.
Dear brothers and sisters,
this is the deepest sorrow of the whole passage.
Truth is not an abstract idea.
Truth was standing right in front of him.
Jesus had said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
(John 14:6)
The One who is Truth Himself
was standing there bound,
two steps away from him.
He asked the right question.
And walked away.
In the original language,
Pilate’s tone
does not sound like a hungry seeker.
It sounds more like a man who has seen it all,
shrugging with a cynical smile:
“Truth? Who talks about truth these days?”
He was not seeking.
He was shutting a door.
I often think of a picture.
There is a kind of child
who likes to ring people’s doorbells
and run away.
The people inside hear it,
put down what they are doing,
walk to the door,
and open it—
and no one is there.
It is not that the owner refused to open the door.
It is that the one who rang would not wait.
Pilate was the one who rang the doorbell and turned to leave.
The door of heaven was opened for him.
Truth Himself stood at the doorway.
But he was already far away.
Many people today are the same.
They ask:
“What is the meaning of life, really?”
“What happens after we die?”
“Is there a true God in this world?”
They ask sincerely.
But just as you begin to answer,
they change the subject.
They start scrolling on their phone.
They say, “Let’s talk another time.”
The problem is not that they did not ask.
The problem is that they would not stay to hear the answer.
\*\*Truth is never hard to find; people just will not stop.\*\*
Jesus said:
“You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
(John 8:32)
But to know the truth
takes one thing:
stop.
Stay.
Keep listening.
Dear family,
we must be careful ourselves.
We may also ask God a question in prayer,
and then, before He answers,
get up and go busy ourselves.
We may open the Bible and ask, “Lord, what do You want to say to me?”
read three lines,
and when the phone rings,
close it.
Asking without waiting
is the same as not asking.
2. He Found No Guilt, Yet Would Not Stand Firm
In the second half of verse 38,
Pilate went out and told the Jews:
“I find no basis for a charge against him.”
This statement,
in the Gospel of John,
Pilate says this three times.
Three times he declared Him innocent.
Three times.
This was a Roman governor,
seated on the judgment seat,
making a judgment by his own authority.
Under Roman law,
if no guilt was found,
the man should have been released on the spot.
But he did not release Him.
He handed Jesus over step by step,
under the whip,
under the crown of thorns,
and finally onto the cross.
Brothers and sisters,
notice the point here.
Pilate’s tragedy
was not that he did not know.
He knew.
He knew very well.
He even said so publicly three times.
His tragedy was this:
\*\*He knew, yet he would not stand firm.\*\*
James 4:17 says:
“To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.”
We often think sin is “doing what we should not do.”
But the Bible says
sin also includes
knowing what we should do
and not doing it.
Pilate had authority in his hands.
With a single word he could have set Him free.
He also knew it was right.
But he did not do it.
Why?
Because he was afraid.
He was afraid the people would riot.
He was afraid word would reach Rome.
He was afraid he would lose his position.
Later the Jews cried out:
“If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend.”
The moment those words came out,
Pilate completely collapsed.
Proverbs 29:25 says:
“The fear of man brings a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh will be exalted.”
One of the greatest weaknesses a person can have
is fearing people more than fearing God.
We often do the same.
We know a certain word should not be said,
but out of fear of offending someone,
we go along with it anyway.
We know we should stand up and clear something up,
but out of fear of being misunderstood,
we stay silent.
We know we should tell that coworker about our faith,
but out of fear of being labeled,
we keep waiting for a “better time.”
Brothers and sisters,
not standing firm
is also a choice.
Silence
is also taking a position.
Pilate thought he had done nothing.
In fact he had done something—
he had handed the Lord over.
Of the three foundations of the 321 principles,
the first is Jesus is my example,
and the second is the Bible is my standard.
Standard means
it is the ruler.
A ruler does not get longer or shorter because someone is shouting in the room.
What Pilate lacked was not judgment.
He lacked a ruler that does not bend.
His ruler
was public opinion.
It was politics.
It was his own future.
A ruler like that
bends the moment pressure is applied.
3. He Tried to Escape by Technique, Not Settle It by Righteousness
In verse 39,
Pilate proposed a plan:
“But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
This was a very clever calculation.
According to the custom of the time,
at the Passover
the governor would release one prisoner
as a gesture of goodwill toward the Jews.
Pilate thought:
If I put Jesus next to a notorious robber,
the people will surely choose Jesus.
That way I release a man,
I do not offend the chief priests,
and I can say, “You chose it yourselves.”
Responsibility passed off.
Position kept.
Problem solved.
But brothers and sisters,
see one thing clearly.
Pilate was not trying to solve the problem with “righteousness.”
He was trying to escape with “technique.”
He did not ask:
What is right?
He asked:
What is safest for me?
There is an enormous distance between the two.
Let me give an illustration.
Hikers know
that some mountain paths are long and winding.
So people often want to take a shortcut,
leave the marked trail,
and cut straight across.
It looks like it saves a lot of distance.
But those who go that way
often cut into deeper forest,
and then it gets dark,
the fog rolls in,
the phone has no signal,
and in the end they are trapped.
A shortcut is not a shorter road.
A shortcut is often a deeper snare.
Pilate’s technique
did not save him;
it pushed him into an even worse situation.
Because the crowd’s answer
was completely unexpected.
He had thought he was leading this trial.
In the end he discovered
that the one really on trial
was himself.
Dear family,
we often do the same in our difficulties.
We do not pray;
we first look for a way out.
We do not ask God’s heart;
we first calculate people’s reactions.
We do not face the conversation we need to face;
we first think about how to get around it.
We handle things with cleverness
instead of with truth.
In the short run it looks like we got through.
In the long run we will certainly pay a greater price.
The 321 principles say:
Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head.
The head
keeps looking for shortcuts.
The heart
asks one question:
Lord, what do You want me to do in this?
4. Barabbas Set Free, the Innocent Lord Handed Over
Verse 40:
“Then they all shouted again, saying, ‘Not this man, but Barabbas!’ Now Barabbas was a robber.”
Brothers and sisters,
this is the clearest picture of substitution
in the whole Bible.
Let us first get to know Barabbas.
The name “Barabbas” means “son of the father.”
The Bible says he was a robber.
The original word
was commonly used at that time for insurrectionists,
plunderers,
even murderous bandits.
Mark tells us
he was “bound with those who had made insurrection,”
and these rebels “had committed murder in the insurrection.”
(Mark 15:7)
In other words,
Barabbas was a man on death row.
He had a name,
a record,
a sentence.
He was a man who fully deserved to die.
And that morning,
in the same courtyard,
two names were set side by side.
One deserved death.
One was innocent.
The crowd shouted:
“Not this man, but Barabbas!”
And so
the one who deserved death walked out.
The innocent One went up.
Luke puts it very plainly:
Pilate “delivered Jesus up to their will.”
Later the apostle Peter said to the people:
“But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you.”
(Acts 3:14)
I often imagine the scene.
In the prison there was a register.
A register of those condemned to die.
It had the date of execution written on it,
and the number of the cross.
That morning,
someone came in with a pen
and drew a line through the three characters “Barabbas.”
Crossed out.
Then in the same line, in the same place,
he wrote another name:
Jesus.
The prison door opened.
The chains fell to the ground.
When Barabbas walked out,
he did not hear a single word of explanation.
He did not know why.
He only knew:
the place where I was meant to hang
now has someone else on it.
Brothers and sisters,
that day on Golgotha there were three crosses.
The one in the middle
was prepared for Barabbas.
The cross Jesus mounted
was Barabbas’s cross.
Barabbas was the first person in the world to personally experience “Jesus died in my place.”
Not understood as a doctrine.
Experienced in his body.
That day he could truly walk home,
eat,
sleep,
and see the next day’s sun.
And the One who took his place
died.
Now,
I want to say something,
and I ask the family to listen slowly.
\*\*Barabbas is me.\*\*
That cross in the middle
was meant for me.
Isaiah 53:6 says:
“All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
1 Peter 3:18 says:
“Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God.”
The righteous
for the unrighteous.
The innocent
for the one who deserved to die.
This is the gospel.
It is not that I behaved well,
so I was released.
It is not that I changed,
so I was pardoned.
Someone went up in my place.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became good.
Dear family,
if today you feel you are unworthy,
let me tell you:
you were never worthy.
Barabbas was not worthy either.
The gospel was never for those who deserve it.
The gospel is for those who are unworthy
yet loved.
There is one more thing we cannot fail to see.
The crowd’s choice.
“Not this man, but Barabbas.”
They would rather have a visible thug
than a King whose kingdom they could not see.
Because Barabbas made them feel satisfied.
And Jesus
called them to repent.
Human hearts are the same today.
We often would rather have an immediate benefit
than the true Savior.
We would rather have health,
smooth sailing,
and people’s approval
than the Lord who comes to deal with the “self” within me.
We may not shout aloud.
But every choice we make
is answering the same question:
Do I want this man,
or Barabbas?
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Bible Is My Standard, and the Gospel Makes Us Self-Denying
This passage today
shines on two of the foundations of 321 at once.
First, the Bible is my standard.
Pilate asked:
“What is truth?”
In his world,
truth was relative.
The strong decided.
The majority decided.
The situation decided.
So his judgment
turned the moment pressure came.
But the Bible tells us
that truth is not a subjective feeling,
nor the result of a majority vote.
In John 17:17, Jesus prayed:
“Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.”
Truth is the word of God.
Psalm 119:105 says:
“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.”
A lamp to my feet
does not go out because someone outside is shouting.
Brothers and sisters,
if a person has no ruler that does not bend,
his whole life will be pushed around by public opinion,
by emotions,
by self-interest.
Among the three foundations,
the Bible is my standard
means this:
when I make a decision,
I do not first ask “What does everyone think?”
but first ask “What does God say?”
Second, the gospel makes us self-denying.
321 keeps saying:
the old self has a life of self,
and it must become the new self with a life of self-denial.
But “self-denial” does not mean gritting my teeth and pressing myself down.
True self-denial
begins in one place—
under the cross.
When a person truly sees:
that place was meant to be mine,
and the Lord went up in my place.
In that moment,
the “self” has no ground to stand on.
What do I have left to boast about?
What do I have to boast with?
I am a pardoned man on death row.
In Galatians 2:20 Paul says:
“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
Brothers and sisters,
we must see the order clearly.
It is not that I first deny myself
and then become worthy of the gospel.
It is that I first receive the gospel,
and only then can I deny myself.
Through the truth of the gospel,
we are able to be emptied of self.
Once emptied of self,
we can let Jesus be King.
Once Jesus is King,
all the glory
will go to Him.
The day Barabbas walked out of the prison door,
he had nothing,
and nothing to boast of.
That is exactly
what every one of us who believes in the Lord truly is.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, do not be the one who asks but will not wait for the answer. Truth is never hard to find; people just will not stop and listen.
Second, knowing what is right and not doing it is sin. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt, yet still handed the Lord over.
Third, fearing people more than God is the greatest snare. Not standing firm is also a choice; silence is also taking a position.
Fourth, a shortcut is not a shorter road; it is a deeper snare. Those who escape by cleverness end up paying a greater price.
Fifth, Barabbas is me. That cross in the middle was meant for me.
Let Us Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we come before You today with hearts full of thanksgiving and full of shame. Lord, we see that Pilate asked “What is truth?” but would not stop and wait for Your answer; have mercy on us, and do not let us become that kind of people—asking You, but not waiting for You; reading Your word, but not letting Your word deal with us. Take away from our hearts the weakness of fearing people more than You, so that we may stand firm where we should stand, and speak out when we should speak, no longer going around by cleverness, but acting only by Your truth. Lord Jesus, thank You: the one who walked out of the prison door that day was Barabbas, and the One who went up onto the cross was You; that middle place was meant for me, yet You went up in my place. We have nothing to boast of, and can only bow down and worship. We ask that You would set us free every day by the truth of the gospel, so that the “self” within us would retreat day by day, and You would be King in us, and everything we do in our lives would bring glory to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. Is there something lately that you already know God wants you to do, but you keep delaying taking a stand because you fear what others will think? What small step are you willing to take today?
2\. If the cross in the middle was meant to be your place, how should this awareness change the way you see yourself, others, and the Lord today?

v: So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him.
The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.
Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!”

When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves, and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”
b: Yesterday we read that Pilate wanted to release Jesus.
Today what we see
is the process of his stepping down, one step at a time.
From the interrogation,
to the scourging,
to the mocking,
to finally handing the Lord over.
These seven verses are short.
But in them is the deepest darkness of human nature,
and also the deepest humility of the Son of God.
Let us quiet ourselves
and read slowly.
1. Unrighteous Compromise Never Buys Peace
Verse 1 is only one short sentence:
“Then Pilate therefore took Jesus, and flogged him.”
Read in Chinese it sounds quite plain.
But if we know what a Roman flogging was,
we dare not read past it so lightly.
The Roman whip
was no ordinary leather strap.
It was several leather cords,
with pieces of sharp bone
and small bits of iron and lead tied into them.
Every stroke
did not only strike the skin;
it caught the flesh
and tore it away.
In history, many who were scourged
died under the whip
before they ever reached the cross.
And why did Pilate flog Jesus?
Notice,
he himself had just said:
“I find no basis for a charge against him.”
A man he had judged innocent,
and yet he ordered him flogged.
Why?
Because he was working out a plan.
He thought:
perhaps when the crowd sees this man beaten like this,
they will soften,
they will be satisfied,
they will let Him go.
This was a compromise.
He did not dare to release Him,
and did not want to condemn Him,
so he chose the road in the middle.
A little beating,
a little giving way,
each side stepping back a little,
and the matter would pass.
Dear family,
this is the road people take most often.
Not complete evil,
but a little bit of giving way.
Not open betrayal,
but “This should be all right, shouldn’t it?”
But let us see clearly how it ended:
did Pilate’s compromise buy him peace?
No.
Not only were the crowd not satisfied,
they shouted even louder:
“Crucify him! Crucify him!”
Here is a picture that cuts deep.
A man is being blackmailed.
The blackmailer comes asking for money,
and he thinks to himself:
give a little,
a little will get rid of him.
So he pulls out some small change.
And the man takes the money,
and comes back the next day.
And this time the price is higher.
Because he now knows:
this man will give way.
Unrighteous compromise
never stops unrighteousness.
It only tells the other side:
you may take one more step.
Pilate thought the flogging was a middle course.
In fact the flogging was a signal.
It told the crowd:
this governor cannot hold his ground.
Push a little more,
and he will hand the man over.
In our own lives too,
there are often moments like this.
We know very well that something is wrong,
yet we think:
just a little bit should be fine.
We know very well we should stand with the Lord,
but out of fear,
we first give way half a step.
And that half step
often becomes the beginning of the whole road that follows.
Lord, give us courage—
not the courage to be unafraid of people,
but the honesty not to deceive ourselves.
2. He Put the Curse of the Earth on His Own Head
Verse 2:
“The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.”
There are two things in this verse.
One is the thorns.
One is the purple robe.
Let us look at the thorns first.
Thorns in the Bible are not just any plant.
In Genesis 3:17–18,
after man sinned,
God said to Adam:
“Cursed is the ground for your sake;”
“Thorns also and thistles will it bring forth to you.”
From that day,
thorns became a sign.
A sign of sin.
A sign of the curse.
A sign that man and the earth are no longer in harmony.
Every farmer pulling thorns in the field,
every time a hand is pricked until it bleeds,
is in fact experiencing the same thing:
this world
is no longer what it was in the beginning.
And now,
the soldiers wove thorns into a crown
and put it on the head of the Son of God.
They thought they were mocking a false king.
They did not know
they were completing a picture.
The curse
placed on His head.
I often think of a picture.
There is a piece of wasteland
overgrown with thorns.
The owner hires a man to clear it.
The man crouches down
and pulls them out one by one,
clearing patch by patch.
By evening,
the ground is clean
and ready for planting.
And when that man stands up,
both of his palms
are full of thorns.
Full of blood.
The ground is clean;
the thorns are all in him.
Dear family,
this is our Lord.
He came
to remove the curse from this earth.
And the way He removed it
was to drive all the thorns
into Himself.
Galatians 3:13 says:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us;”
That crown of thorns
was no accident.
It was the sign of His mission.
Now look at the purple robe.
In the Roman world,
purple was a very costly color.
The dye was taken from a kind of sea snail,
and it took a great many snails
to dye even a little purple.
So purple was the color of kings,
the color of nobles.
The soldiers put a purple robe on Jesus
to stage a play.
What they meant was:
Don’t you say you are a king?
Then here is a king’s clothing for you.
They were mocking.
But the irony is
that everything they said and did
was true.
He truly is King.
He truly deserves to wear the purple robe.
He truly deserves to wear a crown.
Only that crown
should not have been of thorns.
People may mock the truth,
but they cannot change the truth.
People may treat the King as a joke,
yet the King is still the King.
3. False Worship Most Insults the True King
Verse 3:
“and they kept saying, ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ and they kept slapping him.”
Notice the order of these two actions.
First, “Hail.”
Then, the blows.
First the words of salute.
Then the hands of insult.
“Hail, King of the Jews!”
In the original language,
this was the phrase Romans used to salute Caesar.
It was the highest form of address.
And after saying this highest form of address,
they raised their palms and struck His face.
This is false worship.
False worship is not a lack of fine words.
False worship is saying fine words
while doing the exact opposite.
The mouth calls Him King,
but the hand strikes Him.
The lips honor Him as Lord,
but in life we do not let Him be Lord.
Dear family,
let me say this very honestly:
the most piercing thing about this verse
is not the cruelty of the soldiers.
It is that this scene
is not far from us at all.
On Sunday we sing:
“He is King of kings.”
We sing loudly,
and tears even flow.
Then on Monday morning,
facing a decision,
we say:
Lord, I’ll handle this one myself.
In prayer we say:
Lord, You reign.
Then at home,
at the office,
in our relationships,
we still grip the steering wheel tightly.
This is not to say we do not love the Lord.
It is to say
that the “self” within us
has not truly stepped aside.
The 321 principles say it clearly:
Pride is leaving one’s place, grasping power, and wanting to take God’s place.
Humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place.
Let man be man, and let God be God.
The soldiers’ problem was not that they could not speak words of honor.
They could.
Their problem was this:
they would not treat the King as King.
Today we too must ask ourselves:
Is what I call the Lord,
and how I obey the Lord,
the same thing?
If not,
then let us ask the Lord for mercy.
Because the Lord does not need our pleasant words.
What the Lord wants is our throne.
4. Behold the Man
Verses 4–5:
“Pilate went out again, and said to them, ‘Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.’”
“Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, ‘Behold, the man!’”
“Behold the man.”
In the Latin version this sentence is:
Ecce Homo.
For two thousand years,
countless painters have painted this scene,
countless poets have written this line.
When Pilate said it,
what he had in mind was really quite simple.
He wanted to stir pity.
What he meant was probably:
Look at Him.
He has already been beaten like this.
A man with a head full of blood,
dressed in a costume,
barely able to stand—
what threat can he possibly be to Rome?
Enough.
Let him go.
Pilate wanted to use this sentence to end a troublesome affair.
He did not know
he had spoken the sentence that all humanity most needs to hear.
Behold the man.
Dear family,
today we really must stop and look.
Look at the thorns on His head;
that is our curse.
Look at the stripes on His body;
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his stripes we are healed.”
Look at His silence under mockery;
that is the humiliation He swallowed for us.
Look at whom He suffered for.
Look at whom He was beaten for.
We must also notice one thing:
the One standing there
was able to resist.
He had said
that He could ask the Father for more than twelve legions of angels.
With one word
He could have laid the soldiers flat on the ground.
But He did not.
He stood.
He let them strike.
He let them laugh.
He did not say a word in His defense.
To have the power to resist and yet not resist,
this is not weakness.
This is the greatest power in the world.
Because holding back anger
is much harder than letting it out.
Because holding back one sentence
is much harder than saying ten.
When someone without power does not move,
that is helplessness.
When someone with all power does not move,
that is willing self-sacrifice.
Behold the man.
The One standing there letting people humiliate Him
is the very Lord who created them.
5. The Reason They Condemned Him to Death Was His True Identity
Verses 6–7:
“When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, saying, ‘Crucify him! Crucify him!’”
“The Jews answered him, ‘We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.’”
Here,
the real reason is finally spoken.
Earlier they kept accusing Him of political crimes.
They said He claimed to be a king,
that He opposed Caesar.
That was said for the Romans to hear.
But now,
the mask has come off.
“Because he made himself the Son of God.”
This was what they truly could not accept.
Dear family,
see clearly the weight of this sentence.
The reason they condemned Him to death
was His true identity.
They said:
because He claims to be the Son of God,
He must die.
And the fact is:
He truly is the Son of God.
They did not state the facts wrongly.
They only stood on the wrong side.
The same fact
is salvation to those who believe,
and a charge to those who do not.
It is still the same today.
The reasons people reject the Lord
are often the very reasons the Lord is Lord.
Some say:
I cannot accept a faith that asks me to hand over all control.
But being fully Lord
is exactly what it means that He is Lord.
Some say:
I cannot accept something as cruel as the cross.
But the cross
is exactly the proof that God loved us to the end.
The very point we reject
is often the very point we need most.
So today we ask the Lord,
not to change the gospel into what we like,
but to change our hearts
into hearts able to receive the truth.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Humility Overcomes Pride, Self-Denial Overcomes Satan
This passage today
is really a contest between two powers.
On one side is pride.
Pilate’s pride
was clinging to power
yet unwilling to use power to do justice.
The chief priests’ pride
was clinging to the law
yet using the law to kill the God who gave the law.
The soldiers’ pride
was clinging to a moment’s authority
and throwing their weight around before a bound man.
The expressions of pride differ,
but the root is the same:
leaving one’s place, grasping power, wanting to take God’s place.
On the other side is humility.
The Lord Jesus’ humility
was not because He had no power.
It was because He laid power down.
He was scourged, and did not strike back.
He was mocked, and did not answer back.
He was falsely accused, and did not defend Himself.
He was crowned with thorns, and did not take them off.
This is self-denial.
Self-denial is not having no power;
it is having power and not using it for oneself.
Self-denial is not cowardice;
it is placing oneself completely within the Father’s will.
We often say:
Pride provokes pride, and both are hurt.
Humility draws out humility, and both win.
We see
that that night’s pride really did provoke greater pride.
When Pilate stepped back one step,
the crowd stepped forward one.
When the crowd shouted once,
Pilate stepped back again.
A whole crowd pushing one another downward,
until in the end they nailed an innocent man to the cross.
That was a complete loss for everyone.
But what about the Lord’s humility?
The Lord’s humility did not stop there.
What did His humility bring forth?
It brought forth
the melting of tens of thousands of hardened hearts over two thousand years.
It brought forth countless enemies turned into children.
It brought forth you and me,
able to sit here today
and call the mocked King my Lord.
Humility overcame pride.
Self-denial overcame Satan.
Not with a louder voice,
not with greater force,
but with the posture of one willing to bow low.
Dear family,
if today we are stuck in some relationship,
in some dispute where neither side will give way,
remember this scene.
True victory
has never been about who shouts louder.
True victory
is in the Lord who wore the crown of thorns
and did not say a word.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, unrighteous compromise does not buy peace. When Pilate gave one step, the crowd took one; giving way never stops unrighteousness.
Second, the Lord put the curse of the earth on His own head. The thorns are the sign of sin; He bore them Himself so that we might be free.
Third, false worship most insults the true King. Calling Him King with our mouths while not letting Him be Lord in our lives is something we must deal with every day.
Fourth, behold the man. What we are to look at today is not someone else’s fault, but for whom He suffered and for whom He was beaten.
Fifth, the reasons people reject the Lord are often the very reasons the Lord is Lord. What we ask the Lord to change is not the gospel, but our hearts.
Let Us Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see today Your Son scourged, mocked, and crowned with thorns. Lord, we could hardly bear to look at this scene, because those stripes should have fallen on us, and that crown of thorns should have been on our heads. Forgive us: we too, like Pilate, often make unrighteous compromises just to keep the peace; we too, like those soldiers, call You King with our mouths while still gripping our own power with our hands. Take away the pride within us, and let us learn Your humility; deal with the self within us, and let Jesus truly be King in us. When we are misunderstood and looked down on, remind us of Your silent endurance, that we may not win by temper but win people by humility. May we fix our eyes on this man all our lives, and let others see this man in us. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. Is there something lately that you know is wrong, yet you comfort yourself with “just give a little”? Where does the Lord ask you to stand firm again today?
2\. “Behold, the man!” If you quietly gaze today at the Lord wearing the crown of thorns, how would His humility, so powerful yet not resisting, change your attitude toward the difficulty before you?

v: When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid.
He entered into the Praetorium again, and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
Pilate therefore said to him, “Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you and have power to crucify you?”
Jesus answered, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
b: Today’s passage is only four verses.
But these four verses
are the head-on meeting of authority with authority in the whole Gospel of John.
On one side is the governor of the Roman Empire,
holding the power of life and death in his hand.
On the other is one who has been scourged,
crowned with thorns,
and bound by the hands: Jesus.
Judging by outward appearance,
one is standing,
and one is standing in the dock.
But when you finish reading these four verses, you will find:
the one who is truly trembling
is the one who is standing.
1. The Man Who Held the Greatest Power Was the Most Afraid in His Heart
Verse 8:
“When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid.”
What saying had he heard?
In the previous verse,
the Jews cried out:
He made himself the Son of God.
The moment those words reached Pilate’s ears,
he was afraid.
Why afraid?
Because in the Roman world,
“son of God” was not an empty phrase.
Their legends had stories of gods taking human form
and walking among men.
Their emperors were also called sons of God.
Pilate suddenly realized:
this One I am trying today,
could He be no ordinary man?
And he was already uneasy.
Matthew records that
that very morning his wife had sent word to warn him:
have nothing to do with that righteous man.
So the words “more afraid”
mean:
he was afraid already,
and now he was more afraid.
Dear family,
look carefully at this picture.
A governor holding the power of life and death.
A man who could decide with one word whether someone lived or died.
A man whose face all Jerusalem had to watch.
Yet in his heart he was afraid.
He was afraid of this prisoner’s origin.
He was afraid of the shouting of the crowd outside.
He was afraid word would reach Rome.
He was afraid he would lose his position.
He had everything,
yet he was afraid of everything.
Here is a truth that cuts deep:
power can never give a person peace.
The more a person grasps,
the less secure he actually feels.
Have you ever seen a person
crossing the street with his arms full?
He is carrying a tall stack of boxes,
with a bag clamped under his arm,
and a package pressed under his chin.
