v: After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty.”
Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
b: Today’s three verses
sit at the very center of the whole Bible.
From the day in Genesis 3 when man sinned,
the salvation God prepared
has travelled on for thousands of years.
The altar,
the Passover,
the tabernacle,
the priests,
the prophets—
every type and shadow pointed to one moment.
That moment
is found in these three verses.
The Lord Jesus spoke one sentence on the cross:
“It is finished!”
This one sentence
changed the destiny of all humanity.
1. The Lord who made the rivers says, “I thirst”
Verse 28,
Jesus said,
“I am thirsty.”
This is the fifth saying the Lord spoke on the cross.
Let us stop
and think carefully about these words.
The One who said them
is the very Lord who once said, “Let there be light.”
He is the Lord who divided the Red Sea.
He is the Lord who brought water out of the rock in the wilderness.
He is the Lord who said to the Samaritan woman, “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst.”
The rivers were made by Him.
The oceans were made by Him.
Every cloud in the heavens,
every spring on the earth,
are in His hand.
And now,
He hangs on a piece of wood,
His lips cracked and dry,
saying,
I am thirsty.
Dear family,
this is not a word of weak complaining.
It is the truest proof of the incarnation.
He was not wearing human clothing to act out a play.
He truly became a man.
He truly had flesh and blood.
He truly could bleed.
He truly could hurt.
He truly could thirst.
He went through the limits of the human body.
From being seized in the early morning,
to being scourged,
mocked,
and nailed to the cross,
more than twelve hours had passed.
Blood loss,
dehydration,
scorching sun.
That “thirst”
was suffering real to the uttermost.
And why did He go through all of this?
Hebrews 4:15 says:
“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities,”
“but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.”
So when you are so tired today that you don’t want to speak,
when your body aches,
when you lie awake at night,
when you feel that no one understands your struggle—
remember,
there is One who understands completely.
He is not standing far off in heaven, merely sympathizing with you.
He walked through it Himself.
He has been thirsty.
And,
there is an even deeper layer.
Verse 28 says:
“that the Scripture might be accomplished, said, ‘I am thirsty.’”
Psalm 69:21 had already written:
“I was thirsty, and they gave me vinegar to drink.”
A line of poetry written a thousand years earlier
was, at this very moment,
fulfilled without one word missing.
In the midst of excruciating pain,
what was on Jesus’ heart
was still the Father’s word.
To His very last breath,
He was fulfilling the Scriptures.
2. The vinegar on the hyssop—the Lamb of God accomplishing the true Passover
Verse 29,
there is a detail
we can easily read past:
“So they put a sponge full of vinegar on hyssop, and held it to his mouth.”
Hyssop.
Why hyssop?
Hyssop is a small, low plant
with a very thin stem,
not really suited to lifting a soaked sponge.
If it were only a matter of handing something up,
a reed
or a stick would have served far better.
But the Holy Spirit, through John,
deliberately recorded these words.
Because in the Jewish memory,
hyssop belonged to one thing only.
Exodus 12:22 says:
“You shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and strike the lintel and the two door posts with the blood.”
That night,
the Israelites killed the lamb,
dipped the hyssop in the blood,
and put it on the doorframes of their homes.
When the destroying angel saw the blood,
he passed over that house.
That was the first Passover.
Fifteen hundred years later,
in the same city,
at noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover,
the Passover lambs were being slaughtered in the temple,
and outside the city at Golgotha,
someone took up a stalk of hyssop
and reached it toward the Lamb of God.
This is no coincidence.
When John the Baptist first saw Jesus, he said:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
(John 1:29)
On that day,
the true Passover was fulfilled.
Once, the blood of a lamb was put on the doorframe
and spared a household from death.
Now the blood of God’s Son flows on the cross
and spares all who believe from eternal destruction.
Once, it happened once a year.
Now, it is once for all.
Dear family,
our God never acts on a whim.
He began laying the road thousands of years ago.
One unremarkable stalk of hyssop
spans fifteen hundred years
and stitches the Exodus and Golgotha together.
He does not overlook even a detail this small.
How could He possibly forget your struggle today?
3. “It is finished”—the “Paid in Full” stamped on the bill of debt
Verse 30
is the weightiest sentence in the whole Bible:
“It is finished!”
In the original there is only one word:
tetelestai.
In the Greek world of that day,
this word was in use every day.
It was not a religious term.
It was a business term.
When a man owed a debt,
the creditor held a promissory note.
On the day the debt was fully repaid,
the creditor wrote this word on that note—
tetelestai.
It meant:
Paid.
Paid in full.
Owed no more.
So when Jesus cried out on the cross,
it was not “I am done for.”
It was not the final wail of a loser.
It was a victor’s declaration:
Accomplished.
And,
the tense in the original is the perfect tense.
The perfect tense means:
achieved once,
and its effect continues to the present.
It is not “it was finished back then, but who knows about now.”
It is “it was accomplished that one time, and it is still in force today.”
When I was young I saw a village general store.
On the owner’s desk lay a thick ledger.
When the villagers were short of cash,
for rice,
oil,
or salt,
they would first have it written in the ledger.
Entry after entry,
packed tightly,
heavy to look at.
At the end of the year,
when someone brought the money,
the owner would turn to that page,
draw a line from top to bottom,
and write the character for “settled” beside it.
From that moment,
every word on that page was still there,
but not one item could be collected from him again.
Because that account
was settled.
Dear family,
what Jesus cried out on the cross
was that word “settled.”
Everything you have owed in your whole life,
those you remember,
those you dare not think about,
those you assume God could never forgive,
are all on that page.
And He, with His own blood,
drew the line through that page.
4. What did “It is finished” actually accomplish?
That one cry, “It is finished,”
accomplished at least four things.
First, the debt of sin was paid.
Not discounted.
Not postponed.
Not put on installments.
Paid in full.
Second, the demands of the law were satisfied.
The law says the one who sins must die.
The law was not wrong;
we simply could not measure up.
Now the Lord died in our place,
and for those who believe in Him,
the law has nothing left to accuse.
Third, all the types of the Old Testament were fulfilled.
The sheep on the altars,
the sacrifices offered year after year that could not take away sin,
the words the prophets spoke but did not themselves understand—
all lined up at this very moment.
Fourth, the barrier between man and God was torn down.
At the very moment Jesus breathed His last,
something happened in the temple.
Matthew 27:51 says:
“Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.”
That curtain was thick and tall,
separating off the Most Holy Place.
Only the high priest could enter once a year,
and he had to bring blood.
That curtain told people:
You may not come in.
And it was torn.
Notice the direction—
from top to bottom.
It was not torn from below by man.
It was torn from above by God.
God Himself opened that door
and said:
Child, come home.
So listen carefully:
\*\*Salvation is not something man accomplishes, and nothing needs to be added to it.\*\*
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.”
I know an elder
who carried a mortgage for twenty years in his youth.
The day the last payment was made,
the bank sent a certificate of full repayment,
and he went to the land office to have the lien struck from the title deed.
From that day on,
that house was completely his.
The interesting thing is this:
even if he took money to the bank again,
the bank would not accept it.
Because there is no debt left.
Dear family,
what we so often do
is run back to the bank with money,
wanting to make a few more payments.
We try with more effort,
more service,
more self-reproach,
to make up for a debt that was paid long ago.
The Lord said on the cross:
Settled.
All a person can do
is believe
and receive.
5. He bowed His head and gave up His spirit
The last sentence:
“He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.”
Notice the order in the original.
When ordinary people die,
they breathe their last first,
and then the head drops.
But John records the order this way:
first He bowed His head,
and then He gave up His spirit.
This one small order of events
shows something great:
His life was not taken from Him by death.
He gave it up Himself.
Jesus had said long before:
“No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.”
The cross was not an accident.
It was not a good man killed by bad men.
It was not a plan that failed.
It was the Son of God,
in His own appointed time,
after confirming that “all things were now finished,”
calmly bowing His head
and placing His spirit into the Father’s hands.
He did not die like a prisoner.
He died like a king.
A king who had completed His mission
and only then put away His weapons.
And the act of “committing”
is complete trust.
In the darkest hour,
rejected by men,
the Father’s face hidden for a time,
He still placed Himself into the Father’s hands.
Dear family,
what we must learn all our lives
is this one act.
To give ourselves over.
Into His hands.
The Light of the 321 Principles—Through the truth of the gospel, we are able to be emptied of self
Today’s passage
digs out the deepest root of the 321 principles.
We often say:
Self-denial lets Jesus live within us.
Self-denial lets Jesus be King.
Self-denial lets us be led by the Holy Spirit.
Self-denial lets us overcome.
But when many people hear this,
their first reaction is:
“Then I must try harder at self-denial.”
“I must put myself to death with more force.”
So they begin to grit their teeth,
to practice asceticism,
to blame themselves,
and constantly review how they are not good enough.
After several years,
they are more weary than before
and have even less joy.
Why?
Because that kind of “self-denial”
is still relying on self.
It uses the strength of self
to deal with self.
That is a battle that can never be won.
True self-denial
has only one foundation,
and it is this sentence:
\*\*“It is finished.”\*\*
I no longer have to fight for anything for myself,
because the Lord has already accomplished everything for me.
I no longer have to prove I am worthy,
because the account on that page has been settled.
I no longer have to trade performance for God’s acceptance,
because the curtain has been torn from top to bottom.
When a person truly believes “It is finished,”
the self within him that has been struggling,
guarding,
and proving itself
finally lets go.
The truth of the gospel comes in first,
and then the “self” goes out.
This order cannot be reversed.
It is not that I deny myself first
and then the Lord accomplishes it.
It is that the Lord has already accomplished it,
and so I can deny myself.
That is why Galatians 2:20 says:
“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
First there is “crucified with Him,”
and then “Christ lives.”
First there is the “It is finished” on the cross,
and then the “no longer I” in life.
Dear family,
do not walk again the old road of relying on your own performance
and your own asceticism.
The Lord has already walked that road to its end,
and made it through.
What we are to do
is stand on His finished work,
lay down power,
return to our rightful place,
let Jesus be King,
and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, the Lord truly became a man and truly thirsted. So He completely understands the weakness and weariness of our bodies.
Second, the vinegar on the hyssop fulfilled the true Passover. God’s plan spans a thousand years and misses not one detail.
Third, “It is finished” means paid in full, not “it’s over.” Accomplished once, valid forever, with nothing left to collect.
Fourth, the curtain torn from top to bottom was torn by God’s own hand. Salvation is not something man accomplishes, and nothing needs to be added to it.
Fifth, He bowed His head first and then gave up His spirit. His life was not taken from Him; He laid Himself down like a king.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we bow down before the cross and worship Your only beloved Son, Jesus Christ. Lord, You are the One who made the rivers and the oceans, yet on the wood You said, “I am thirsty”; You are the holy and glorious God, yet You were willing to have vinegar lifted to You on a stalk of hyssop. Thank You for becoming the true Passover Lamb and covering us with Your own blood. Lord, thank You for declaring on the cross, “It is finished”—every debt we have owed in our whole lives, You have paid in full; You have drawn the line through that page, and no one can ever collect from us again. Forgive us: we so often refuse to believe that this has been completed, and still want to use our own effort and our own performance to earn the grace You have already freely given. May the Holy Spirit shine on us, so that these two words, “It is finished,” become the only foundation of our life of self-denial. We want to be like You, to bow our heads and place ourselves in the Father’s hands, to let Jesus live within us, to let Jesus be King, and to give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Is there still an account in your heart that you dare not believe the Lord has already cleared? Today, are you willing to hand it over to that word, “It is finished”?
2\. In your present service and life, is there something where you are really “running back to the bank with money”—trying to make up, by your own effort, a debt that has long since been paid?

v: Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him;
but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.
However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.
For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.”
Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”
b: The Lord had breathed His last.
The work on the cross was finished.
By rights,
the story could end here.
But John did not lay down his pen.
He took special note of two things that seem very small:
the soldiers did not break the Lord’s legs;
and one soldier pierced the Lord’s side.
Two small matters,
yet a closing John set down with great care.
Because within these two small matters
we are meant to see two things:
the hand of God,
and the word of God.
1. The shell of religion can stay intact while the inside is empty
Verse 31,
begins with a very heavy sentence:
“Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, … (for that Sabbath was a special one)…”
What were they thinking?
They were thinking:
Tomorrow is the Sabbath,
and the Sabbath of Passover week,
a “high day.”
The bodies must not remain on the crosses overnight.
For Deuteronomy provides
that one who is hanged is under a curse,
and the land God gives must not be defiled.
So they went to Pilate
and asked him to send men to break the criminals’ legs,
so that they would die more quickly
and the bodies could be taken away.
Brothers and sisters,
do you see the irony in this?
They kept the Sabbath rules down to the last detail.
They calculated exactly
which day was the Preparation,
which day was the high day,
and by what hour the bodies had to be dealt with.
Yet what they were in the very act of doing
was killing the Lord of the Sabbath.
They were busy not defiling the land,
but had never considered
that their own hands
were already stained with the blood of God’s Son.
This is not because they were especially wicked.
This is the common disease of religion.
It is like a person who, at New Year, does the great housecleaning,
mops the floor until it shines,
wipes the windows spotless,
and tidies every corner,
yet in all the busyness
leaves the elderly parent off to one side,
never saying a single word to them.
The house is clean.
The home is cold.
The shell of religion can be kept perfectly intact
while the inside has long been empty.
We must be careful too.
We have not missed a meeting,
have not skimped on giving,
have filled out the service forms neatly,
have read all the Scriptures we should.
But is the Lord in our hearts?
Is the Lord in our daily life?
When we make decisions,
do we let the Lord be King?
The 321 principles keep reminding us:
life first,
then relationship,
then ministry.
Once the order is reversed,
we will be like the Jews of that day,
doing religion very well
while leaving the Lord nailed up outside.
The shell can maintain itself,
but life can only come from the Lord.
2. Not one bone broken—even the soldiers’ hands are under God’s control
Verses 32–33:
“Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him;
but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.”
Breaking the legs
was a cruel Roman practice.
Once a crucified man’s legs were broken,
he could no longer push himself up to breathe
and would soon suffocate.
The soldiers went in order.
The first man: broken.
The second man: broken.
When they came to the One in the middle,
they took a look
and found He was already dead,
and so stopped.
What a casual action.
A soldier,
on one afternoon,
took a glance
and decided on the spot not to strike.
He could not have known what he was doing.
He could not have known
that by holding back his hand
he was fulfilling the regulation God set fifteen hundred years before.
For Exodus 12:46 says of the Passover lamb:
“You shall not break a bone of it.”
Numbers 9:12
says the same thing again.
The Passover lamb
could be killed,
could shed blood,
could be roasted with fire,
but not one bone was to be broken.
And the first thing John the Baptist said as he pointed to Jesus was:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
(John 1:29)
Now,
the true Passover Lamb hangs on the cross.
He was killed.
He shed His blood.
But His bones,
not one of them was broken.
Dear family,
think carefully about this.
God did not use a miracle to stop the soldiers.
No angel appeared.
No voice came from heaven.
God simply let that soldier “take a glance.”
Even the passing decision of a Gentile soldier
is within His control.
We often think
that God only manages the big things.
We think God only steps in at the great turning points.
But it is not so.
God governs down to the smallest places.
He governs even a single thought of a person.
He governs whether one movement stops or goes on.
So then,
what about that thing you are worrying about today?
That link you cannot control at all?
That juncture where the decision rests in someone else’s hands?
If God governs even the iron rod in a soldier’s hand,
would He not govern your tomorrow?
The 321 principles say:
the focus is on Jesus,
not on self,
not on others,
not on circumstances.
Because circumstances were never the ruler.
The Ruler is the God who sits on the throne.
3. Blood and water came out—He truly died
Verse 34:
“However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.”
What was this spear thrust for?
By Roman soldiers’ custom,
it was the final confirmation.
They had to be certain the prisoner was really dead
before they could report back.
And after the spear went in,
what came out was not blood alone,
but “blood and water.”
From a medical point of view,
this is a sign that a person has truly died.
The fluid around the heart separated from the blood,
and the blood no longer circulated.
In other words,
this one thrust
was, in effect, the death certificate for the Lord’s death.
The Lord was not unconscious.
The Lord was not feigning death.
The Lord was not taken down from the cross
and revived a few days later.
The Lord truly died.
Brothers and sisters,
this point is extremely important.
Because if He did not truly die,
there was no true resurrection.
If there was no true resurrection,
our faith is in vain.
The foundation of the gospel is not a feeling,
it is a fact:
He truly died,
He was truly buried,
and He truly rose on the third day.
And many interpreters
have also seen in this “blood and water”
two sides of salvation.
Blood is for the penalty that washes away sin.
Water is for cleansing the defilement of life.
Blood deals with my past.
Water deals with my present.
Blood makes me without guilt before God;
water makes me renewed in daily life.
Many of us have received only half.
We believe the Lord’s blood has washed away our sins,
yet we often forget
that the same Lord
also washes our daily life clean with water, day by day.
Being saved is not the finish line.
Being saved is the starting point.
What flowed from that side
was not only forgiveness,
but also a new life.
4. “That you may believe”—the gospel is not a legend but an eyewitness testimony
Verse 35 is very special:
“He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.”
Throughout the whole Gospel of John,
the author is almost always hidden.
He never says “I.”
He calls himself only “the disciple whom Jesus loved.”
But here,
he suddenly steps forward.
It is as if he wants to take the reader by the shoulders and say:
I was there for this.
I saw it with my own eyes.
I know what I am saying.
You can believe.
Why does he stress this so particularly?
Because he knows
that later there will surely be those who say:
“That is only legend.”
“That was added by later people.”
“That was the disciples’ collective imagination.”
So he puts himself forward to bear witness.
It is like a dashcam.
Two cars scrape each other at an intersection,
and each side tells its own story.
You say I ran the red light,
I say you didn’t signal.
They argue until neither will yield.
But once the dashcam footage is pulled up
and the picture plays,
the matter is settled.
Because that is not anyone’s version;
it is the fact recorded on the spot.
What John does here
is hand over that recording.
Dear family,
our faith is not built on emotion,
not built on a lovely imagination,
but on what truly happened in history.
There were people present.
There were people who saw.
There were people who gave their lives to bear witness to it.
And John states the purpose of writing all this:
that you may believe.
5. “They will look on him whom they pierced”—grace hidden within judgment
Verses 36–37,
John quotes two Old Testament passages:
“Not one of his bones will be broken.”
“They will look on him whom they pierced.”
The second is from Zechariah 12:10:
“They will look to me whom they have pierced.”
Notice the weight of this sentence.
Those who pierced Him
will one day look on Him.
There is judgment in this.
For Revelation 1:7 says
that when the Lord comes with the clouds,
every eye will see Him,
even those who pierced Him.
On that day,
no one will be able to hide.
But there is also tremendous grace in it.
Because the word “look,”
in the Old Testament, often carries the meaning of being saved.
When the Israelites were bitten by fiery serpents in the wilderness,
Moses lifted up the bronze serpent,
and everyone who looked lived.
The Lord Himself said,
as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness,
even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.
So the true meaning of this sentence is:
even those who pierced Him
still have the chance to look on Him and be saved.
Brothers and sisters,
who are you and I?
We are the ones who pierced Him.
It was not that Roman soldier who pierced Him;
it was my sin that pierced Him.
It was my pride,
my self,
my rebellion
that drove that spear into His side.
And the blood and water He poured out for us
was meant precisely to wash the very hands that pierced Him.
This is where the gospel is most heartbreaking,
and also most comforting.
The One who was pierced
turned around and became the Savior of those who pierced Him.
The Light of the 321 Principles—Information, Revelation, Conviction
The eight steps of changing a mindset are:
information,
revelation,
conviction,
practice,
review,
correction,
repetition,
multiplication.
Today’s passage
plays out the first three steps for us.
The first step is information.
What John does in verse 35
is place the information in our hands.
The soldiers did not break His legs.
One soldier pierced His side.
Blood and water came out.
These are facts,
information that can be examined
and recounted.
But information alone
does not change a life.
The people standing at the foot of the cross at that time
saw the same information.
The soldiers saw it.
The chief priests saw it.
The crowd of onlookers saw it.
They all saw the same scene,
yet not one of them knelt because of it.
Because information must move on to the second step—revelation.
Revelation is the Holy Spirit driving that fact
into our hearts.
So that we suddenly see:
that was not a condemned criminal;
that was the Lamb of God.
That was not an accident;
that was the salvation God had long ordained.
That was not someone else’s sin;
that was my sin.
This step
cannot be reached by reading more books.
This step is the work of the Holy Spirit.
And only with revelation
do we arrive at the third step—conviction.
Conviction is not “I know this happened.”
Conviction is “I hand myself over.”
John said:
that you may believe.
What he wants is not for us to know one more thing;
he wants us to move from hearing
to believing.
Dear family,
let us ask ourselves honestly:
is my knowledge of the Lord
stuck at information,
or has it entered revelation?
We can explain the whole Gospel of John fluently,
can recite the life of Jesus by heart,
but if all of that is only data in the head,
life will not change in the slightest.
Using the head and relying on self
can only stop at information.
Using the heart and relying on the Holy Spirit
is how we receive revelation.
And the one who has received revelation
will surely go on to conviction,
will surely go on to practice.
Because one who has truly been illumined
cannot live back in the old way.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, do not merely keep the shell of religion looking good. A person who keeps the rules may be locking the Lord outside the door.
Second, God governs even a single thought of a soldier. He governs down to the smallest detail, and He will surely govern your tomorrow.
Third, the blood and water prove the Lord truly died. Without a true death there is no true resurrection; the blood washes away sin, and the water cleanses life.
Fourth, the gospel is an eyewitness testimony, not a legend. Our faith has a solid historical foundation that can withstand questioning.
Fifth, those who pierced Him can still look on Him and be saved. We are the ones who pierced Him, and His blood was shed precisely for us.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that even after Your Son breathed His last, You went on fulfilling Your word step by step. Lord, we see the soldier’s hand stop, we see the spear thrust in, we see blood and water come out, and we know that none of this was by chance; all of it was within Your control and Your promise. Forgive us: we often, like the people of that day, keep the outward rules well while giving You no place in our hearts; and we often stay at information, knowing much, yet not truly illumined by Your revelation, not truly convinced. May the Holy Spirit drive Your word into our hearts, so that we no longer merely hear, but truly believe and truly hand ourselves over. Lord, we are the ones who pierced You, yet we have been washed clean by Your precious blood. May we look to You all our lives, let You be King within us, and give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. In your present life of faith, which part has been left with only the “shell”—going through the motions without the Lord’s presence? Which one thing are you willing to begin handing back to the Lord?

2\. Of everything you know about Jesus, which piece of “information” has not yet become “revelation” struck into your heart? How can you ask the Holy Spirit today to turn it into conviction and practice?

v: After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body.
Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds.
So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand) they laid Jesus there.
b: The matter of the cross was over.
The Lord had breathed His last.
At this moment,
two names appear.
Not Peter.
Not James.
Not the twelve who had followed at the Lord’s side for three years.
But two men who had always been hiding in the shadows.
On the surface, today’s passage
is only a record of a burial.
But hidden within it is a very deep lesson.
1. The cross reveals the true condition of every person
Let us first look at something very strange.
The disciples who had followed the Lord openly for three years
were, at this moment,
nowhere to be found.
The Gospels tell us
they had scattered.
Peter followed at a distance,
and then denied the Lord three times.
The rest of the disciples
hid in a house
with the doors shut.
Yet at that very same time,
two men who had never dared to be public
stepped forward.
One was Joseph of Arimathea.
The other was Nicodemus.
The Bible says it plainly:
Joseph was “a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews.”
Nicodemus
was “the one who at first came to Jesus by night.”
These two men,
one afraid of people,
one who walked in the dark.
They were the two who hid the deepest.
Yet once the cross was raised,
the order was entirely reversed.
Dear family,
the cross has a power.
It makes plain the true condition inside every person.
What cannot be seen ordinarily
can be seen there.
Those who ordinarily speak loudest
suddenly have no voice there.
Those who ordinarily dared not speak
suddenly stand up there.
Because before the cross,
all performances stop.
All titles lose their force.
What remains
is only whether you truly love Him in your heart.
We often think
the test of faith is in the church.
But the real test
is when no one speaks up for you.
It is when following the Lord costs you something.
It is when following the Lord no longer seems to bring any benefit.
Whether you are still there then
is what is real.
2. The Lord did not cast away the one who was a disciple in secret
Verse 38 has a sentence
that is painful to read:
“a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews.”
It is easy to look down on such a person.
We think he is not brave enough.
We think he is not loyal enough.
We think he does not believe thoroughly enough.
But notice that
the Holy Spirit does not rebuke him here.
The Holy Spirit simply records honestly:
he was a disciple of Jesus.
He feared people.
So he was a disciple in secret.
\*\*Joseph was not a false disciple; he was a disciple who did not yet have courage.\*\*
The difference here is enormous.
A false disciple has no Lord in his heart at all.
A disciple without courage
has the Lord in his heart
and simply has not yet reached that step.
The Lord knew He was in his heart.
So the Lord did not cast him away.
Not only did He not cast him away,
but at the end,
at the most critical moment,
the moment no one dared come forward,
the Lord used him.
If Joseph had not gone to ask Pilate that day,
the Lord’s body would have been thrown into the criminals’ common burial pit.
Then the prophecy of Isaiah,
“They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death,”
could not have been fulfilled.
God waited three years,
letting a timid man slowly grow up.
Then on the day it was most needed,
He placed the whole matter in his hands.
Dear family,
if you feel today that you are that Joseph,
believing in your heart,
but not daring to speak at work,
not daring to speak at the family gathering,
not daring to admit before classmates that you are a Christian—
I want to tell you one thing:
the Lord sees that He is in your heart.
The Lord will not strike you off because you are still timid.
He will give you time to grow.
And He will surely, one day,
give you an opportunity
to stand up.
The question is not how brave you are today.
The question is whether you keep staying beside Him.
3. Life change often comes step by step
Nicodemus appears three times in the Gospel of John.
When we set these three times side by side,
we see something beautiful.
The first time,
in chapter 3.
He was a ruler of the Jews,
a Pharisee.
He came to Jesus,
but he came “by night.”
Coming by night
meant he did not want to be seen.
That time,
Jesus said to him:
“Unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
The second time,
in chapter 7.
The council wanted to condemn Jesus,
and Nicodemus said a sentence:
“Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?”
He said it very carefully.
He did not say, “I believe in Him.”
He only spoke of procedure,
of the law,
trying to win a bit of fairness for Jesus.
He spoke only half a sentence.
And then he was shot down by his colleagues.
The third time
is today’s passage.
This time,
it was not night.
It was broad daylight.
He was not speaking half a sentence.
He came with a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes,
and with his own hands embraced that crucified body.
Three appearances,
each one closer than the last.
From night
to day.
From hiding
to coming forward.
From half a sentence
to his whole self.
Dear family,
the dawn does not come all at once.
We seldom see night turn to noon with a snap.
Dawn begins with a little paleness in the sky,
then the east slowly turns red,
and only then does the sun rise.
If you look at three in the morning,
you would think day would never come.
But as long as the direction does not change,
day will surely come.
Life change is like that too.
Many people think they must become another person overnight.
Then after three months they see no progress in themselves,
and they lose heart
and give up.
The 321 principles say:
the eight steps for changing a mindset are information,
revelation,
conviction,
practice,
review,
correction,
repetition,
multiplication.
Notice that “repetition.”
Change takes repetition.
It does not happen all at once.
Nicodemus walked for three years.
From night to day,
it took three years.
If you look back
and find you are a little closer to the Lord than last year,
that is right.
Do not despise that little bit.
That is the dawn coming.
4. True faith comes at a cost
We must know who these two men were.
Joseph of Arimathea,
Luke tells us, was a member of the council,
that is, of the Jewish Sanhedrin.
Nicodemus,
John chapter 3 says, was “a ruler of the Jews,”
also a member of the council.
And the very body that had just condemned Jesus to death
was this council.
Now,
two prominent men of the council:
one goes to the Roman governor to ask for the body of a man executed for “insurrection,”
the other walks into the place of execution in broad daylight carrying a hundred pounds of spices.
What did this mean at that time?
It meant:
their careers were over.
Their standing was gone.
There was no going back before their colleagues.
And under Jewish custom,
touching a corpse made one unclean,
and they could not eat the Passover feast.
At the most important feast of the year,
they willingly let themselves be shut out.
This is not a passing feeling;
this is a cost.
Today we often speak of faith too cheaply.
As if believing in the Lord means a moment of believing in the heart
and one sentence of confession with the mouth.
But faith in the Bible
has always made people pay something.
Abraham’s faith
made him leave his country and his kindred.
Moses’ faith
made him give up the palace of Egypt.
The faith of these two council members
made them lose, in a single day, half a lifetime’s work.
Look again at the hundred pounds.
A hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes
was the standard for burying a king.
An ordinary family burying a loved one
needed only a little spice.
A hundred pounds
is an extremely costly,
nearly extravagant amount.
Why did Nicodemus use so much?
Because he knew in his heart who He was.
He was not burying a failed rabbi.
He was burying a King.
How a person gives
shows how he sees that One in his heart.
What we give the Lord
is not a financial question;
it is a question of knowing Him.
When a person truly sees that He is King,
giving no longer needs to be forced.
5. The new tomb in the garden
Verses 41–42,
the Holy Spirit takes special note of three details.
First,
it was a garden.
Second,
in the garden there was a new tomb.
Third,
that tomb was one “in which no man had ever yet been laid.”
None of these three details was written casually.
First look at the garden.
The fall of mankind
began in a garden.
In the Garden of Eden,
man listened to the serpent
and wanted to be like God.
That was the beginning of “self,”
the beginning of pride,
the beginning of leaving one’s place
and wanting to take God’s.
And now,
the completion of salvation
is also in a garden.
In this garden,
the Lord who obeyed to the end
and was completely emptied of self
was laid in a tomb.
In the first garden,
man reached out and took fruit he should not have taken.
In this garden,
God gave up His own Son.
Now look at the tomb.
“A new tomb, in which no one had ever yet been laid.”
When the Lord Jesus came into the world,
He was born in someone else’s manger.
He rode on someone else’s donkey colt.
His last supper
was set in someone else’s upper room.
After He died,
He was buried in someone else’s tomb.
He had nothing of His own on earth.
Yet this borrowed tomb
He used for only three days.
On the third day,
He returned it.
And He returned it empty.
Brothers and sisters,
this is the greatest comfort in reading this passage today.
At that time,
when Joseph and Nicodemus rolled the stone into place,
they surely thought
that everything was over.
They were carrying out their last act of devotion in despair.
They did not know
that it was not a period at the end.
It was only three days.
In our own lives,
we too sometimes come to a place
where it seems all we can do is arrange the funeral for something.
A relationship.
A hope.
A person we have prayed for over many years.
But remember:
the place you think is a tomb,
with God,
may be only three days.
The Light of the 321 Principles—2-3-5: Two who hid became each other’s companions
Today’s passage
shows us something very precious.
Joseph and Nicodemus
were originally two people each hiding on his own.
One feared people
and was a disciple in secret.
One walked in the dark,
groping in the night to ask about the truth.
Had each been alone,
I think they probably would not have stepped forward.
One person hiding
hides all the deeper.
But this time,
they walked together.
One went to claim the body.
One brought the spices.
One took on facing Pilate.
One took on preparing the burial.
The two together
did what everyone else dared not do.
The 321 principles say:
develop 2 spiritual companions,
establish 3 spiritual parents and children,
become a team of 5 spiritual comrades.
This is not an organizational chart.
This is the reality of life.
There is a very heavy table,
and no matter how one person lifts, it cannot be moved.
He puts all his back into it,
and the legs of the table still won’t leave the floor.
But with two people, one at each end,
a gentle lift
and it comes up.
It is not that the table became lighter.
It is that someone shared the weight.
Spiritual things are like this too.
One person facing pressure
shrinks smaller and smaller.
Two facing it together
find their courage.
\*\*A spiritual companion makes a person brave.\*\*
Do you have such a 2?
Is there anyone
to whom you can say,
“I am actually very afraid in my heart”—
that person?
If not,
ask the Lord to prepare one for you.
If you do,
cherish him,
and do not let that line be cut.
And why were these two able to come together?
Because at that moment,
their “self” had disappeared.
They were not arguing over who would lead.
They were not counting who gave more spices.
They did not care whose rank was higher.
Their eyes were on One alone—
the Lord who had been crucified.
The 321 principles say:
self-denial makes oneness possible.
As long as “self” is still there,
fellow workers turn into fellow attackers.
Serving together
only wounds more deeply.
But when everyone’s focus is on Jesus,
oneness happens naturally.
It is not that we strive for oneness.
It is that we together are emptied of self,
and oneness is simply there.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, the cross reveals the true condition of every person. The real test is not in the meeting but when following the Lord costs something.
Second, the Lord did not cast away the one who was a disciple in secret. God gives people time to grow; just keep staying beside Him.
Third, life change often comes step by step. Dawn does not come all at once, but if the direction is right, it will surely come.
Fourth, true faith pays a cost. How a person gives shows how he sees that One in his heart.
Fifth, the place you think is a tomb may be only three days with God. The Lord used even a borrowed tomb for only three days and returned it empty.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for leaving the names of these two men at the foot of the cross, so that we know You do not cast away the timid. Lord, within us there is often Joseph’s fear and Nicodemus’s hesitation; we believe in our hearts, yet do not dare to acknowledge You before others. Have mercy on us, remove the self within us that fears people, give us courage, and let us stand up when it is time to stand up. Prepare spiritual companions for us too, so that we no longer hide alone, but can hold each other up and together do what no one can do alone. Lord, let us be like Nicodemus, drawing closer to You each time, walking step by step from night into day. When we meet what seems to be finished, remind us: You used even the tomb for only three days. May we give You the most precious thing we have all our lives, because You are our King, and may all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. In your life right now, which setting is the one where you are least willing to admit you are a Christian? Might the Lord be giving you a chance to stand up today?
2\. Is there a spiritual companion near you with whom you can “lift the table” together? This week, whom could you take the initiative to draw closer to?

v: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.
Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb.
They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.
Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.
For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
So the disciples went away again to their own homes.
b: Let us enter John chapter 20 together.
From chapter 18 to chapter 19,
it is arrest,
trial,
scourging,
the cross,
burial.
All the way, a downward slide.
By chapter 20,
the light of day has not yet come,
yet the whole story turns over.
But what is remarkable is that
John does not begin to record this morning
with shouts of joy.
He begins with tears,
running,
misunderstanding,
and the words, “we don’t know where they have laid him.”
This is a great comfort to us.
Because our faith,
too, is often walked out like this, one step at a time.
1. While it was still dark, love made her rise early
Verse 1 says:
“Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb.”
Notice these words:
while it was still dark.
By Jewish custom,
one did not go out before daylight.
The roads outside the city were unsafe,
and a graveyard was no place for a woman to go in the early morning.
But she went.
Because love does not watch the clock.
Love makes a person rise early.
Love makes a person willing to take a little risk.
Let us ask a question:
why did she go so early?
What was she going to do?
The answer pierces the heart.
She was not going to celebrate the resurrection.
She was going to face death.
She carried spices,
ready to anoint a corpse.
In her heart,
the story of Jesus had ended.
She loved the Lord,
but she had no hope.
Dear family,
this is the true condition of many believers.
We truly love the Lord.
We still read the Word,
still pray,
still gather,
still serve.
But that one thing in our hearts
we have already declared dead.
That child,
we feel will never turn back.
That marriage,
we feel can never be restored.
That body,
that job,
that weakness of many years,
we have already prepared the spices in our hearts,
waiting only to go and anoint a corpse.
The love is still there,
but the hope is gone.
The Lord Jesus did not rebuke Mary.
He let her come to the tomb,
and then gave her a surprise beyond all she asked or imagined.
2. A grieving person easily interprets everything in the worst way
Verse 2,
Mary saw that the stone had been taken away,
and she ran to tell Peter and the others:
“They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
This sentence is worth stopping to think about.
What was the fact?
The fact was that the Lord had risen.
What did she see?
She saw that the stone had been rolled away.
The very same stone
could be interpreted as:
the Lord has come out.
Or it could be interpreted as:
the body has been stolen.
She chose the worst one.
Not because she was bad,
but because she was so grieved.
When a person is grieving,
there is a habit inside:
interpreting everything in the worst direction.
The same words,
when we are in a good mood sound like concern,
and when we are in a bad mood sound like sarcasm.
The same event,
when we have hope we see a turning point,
and when we have no hope we see a dead end.
The angle from which we see things
determines our mood.
And going deeper:
the angle from which we see things
also determines how we see God.
Mary’s conclusion was:
“We don’t know where they have laid him.”
It meant:
even the last little remembrance had been taken from her.
She interpreted a great thing God had done
as a wicked thing done by men.
Have we ever done this?
God is clearly at work,
yet we think we have been abandoned.
God is clearly rolling away the stone,
yet we are weeping over what we have lost.
3. The linen cloths still lay there: the scene of the resurrection had no panic at all
Verses 5–7,
John describes the inside of the tomb with very fine strokes.
“and saw the linen cloths lying.”
“and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.”
These sentences seem plain,
but they are in fact the most powerful evidence in the whole passage.
Let us think:
if someone really had stolen the body,
what would have happened?
First, with time pressing,
they would surely have carried off the body, cloths and all.
Second, if they had to unwrap it,
it would have been done in a panic,
the cloths pulled apart,
dropped on the ground,
in a heap.
It is impossible that someone would slowly roll up the head cloth in the tomb
and set it carefully in a separate place.
There is no sign here of things being ransacked.
Here is quiet,
unhurried,
orderly.
This reminds me of something small.
In summer
we often see on trees the empty shells cicadas have shed.
The shell still clings whole to the trunk,
its shape intact,
a split down the back,
but inside it is empty.
At a glance you know:
no one came to seize it,
no one came to steal it.
The One inside
went out by Himself.
And He went out quietly.
The linen cloths are just like that.
The cloths remained in place,
the head cloth rolled up in another place,
but inside it was empty.
The death that once wrapped Him
was now only an empty shell.
This tells us something extremely important:
at the moment of the resurrection,
there was no panic.
Because death poses no threat to the Lord.
He did not break free with great struggle;
He walked out unhurried.
In Gethsemane He sweated as it were great drops of blood,
on the cross He was nailed,
mocked,
and forsaken;
but in the tomb,
He was not at all flustered.
He even rolled up the head cloth.
Dear family,
the Lord in whom we believe,
entered death willingly,
and overcame death with ease.
4. Saw and believed, yet did not yet understand the Scripture
Verse 8 says:
“So the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.”
Verse 9 follows immediately:
“For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise again from the dead.”
These two verses side by side
are very honest.
John believed because he saw the evidence.
He saw the empty tomb,
saw the rolled-up head cloth,
and suddenly it dawned on him:
He really is alive.
But he himself admits:
at that time they did not yet understand that the Scripture had said this long before.
In fact the Lord Jesus had said it with His own mouth several times.
Matthew 16:21 says:
“From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up.”
The angels also reminded the women on resurrection day:
“He isn’t here, but is risen.”
(Luke 24:6)
The words had been spoken long before.
They had simply not taken them in.
We are often like this:
we experience first,
and only afterward understand that the Scripture had said it all along.
We hurt first,
and only then turn back to find that verse was there all along.
We go a long way around first,
and only then remember that the Lord had reminded us quite clearly.
This is our weakness,
but it is also God’s grace.
Because the Lord did not give up on them for not understanding.
He let them see first,
and then slowly led them to understand.
But we must learn a lesson:
if they had truly understood the Scripture then,
there would have been no tears that morning,
no misunderstanding that “someone has taken the Lord away,”
but a group of people standing before the tomb saying:
“The third day has come, and we are here waiting for Him.”
Not understanding the Scripture,
we are led around by what is before our eyes.
Understanding the Scripture,
we can stand on the promise and look at what is before our eyes.
5. The one who ran faster and the one who went in first—the Lord uses both
Verses 4–8 contain an interesting detail.
“They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.”
John ran faster
and arrived first,
yet “stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying; yet he didn’t enter in.”
Peter came after him,
and “entered into the tomb.”
The two men had completely different temperaments.
John was delicate,
perceptive,
looking clearly before acting.
Peter was impulsive,
direct,
going in the moment he thought of it.
Yet the Holy Spirit writes these two side by side in the same passage,
praising neither
and belittling neither.
Because God uses people of different temperaments.
Some are quick,
some are steady.
Some look first,
some act first.
Some open the road in front,
some finish up behind.
We often make a mistake in the church:
measuring others by our own temperament.
The hasty accuse the slow of having no burden,
and the slow accuse the hasty of not being careful enough.
But on that early morning,
the one who ran faster and the one who went in first,
the Lord used both.
And in the end they both believed.
There is no need to compare with one another.
God made you the way you are
because in His system
He needs someone like you.
The Light of the 321 Principles—The Bible Is My Standard
Today’s passage
is the very one of the three foundations of the 321 principles
that it sets before us:
the Bible is my standard.
Notice this sentence in verse 9:
“For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise again from the dead.”
The Holy Spirit, through John,
personally points out the root of all the confusion of that morning.
It was not that they did not love the Lord.
Mary came while it was still dark,
Peter and John took to their heels and ran;
there was nothing wrong with their love.
The problem was:
they did not understand the Scripture.
So they loved truly,
but panicked deeply.
This gives us a very practical reminder.
Say we buy a new appliance at home.
Sometimes it makes a little noise,
or gives off a smell the first time we use it.
We are startled,
think it is broken,
and rush to make a phone call.
Then we open the manual
and find it was written there all along:
“Normal for first use.”
It is not that the machine had a problem;
it is that we had not read the manual.
The Bible is the word God has given us.
Many times it is not that we have met something God never said,
but that we have met something God said
and we did not understand it.
Understand God’s word first,
and we will not be frightened by the empty tomb before us.
And understanding God’s word
brings one result:
changing the viewpoint can change the mindset.
From a temporary viewpoint
to an eternal viewpoint.
With a temporary viewpoint, looking at that morning,
what we see is:
the stone is rolled away,
the Lord is gone,
everything is over.
With an eternal viewpoint, looking at that morning,
what we see is:
death has been rolled away,
the Lord is alive,
everything is just beginning.
The same empty tomb,
two viewpoints,
two lives.
2 Corinthians 4:18 says:
“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
\*\*What the eyes see is temporary; what God’s word says is eternal.\*\*
So,
when you too have an empty tomb before you,
something you think is already finished,
do not rush to a conclusion.
First go back to God’s word.
Ask:
about this matter,
what has God said?
Because the Lord Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
If He has said it,
it will surely be accomplished.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, one who loves the Lord may still have no hope. Do not face that matter only carrying spices; face it carrying God’s promise.
Second, in grief it is easy to interpret things in the worst way. Do not rush to a conclusion; God may be rolling the stone away.
Third, the scene of the resurrection was quiet and orderly. Death poses no threat to the Lord; the Lord we believe in triumphs with ease.
Fourth, we often experience first and understand the Scripture afterward. Understand God’s word first, and we will not be led around by what is before our eyes.
Fifth, God uses people of different temperaments. There is no need to compare; the way you are has its use in God’s system.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that on that early morning while it was still dark, You had already accomplished the greatest thing. Lord, we confess that we are often like Mary, loving You yet without hope, carrying spices to face something we have already declared dead in our hearts. Forgive us, and heal the heart within us that always thinks the worst. May the Holy Spirit open our understanding so that we understand the Scripture and Your word becomes our true standard; so that we are no longer led around by what we see, but stand on Your promise and look at today’s difficulty with an eternal viewpoint. Lord, You even rolled up the head cloth unhurried; in the tomb You had not a trace of panic; place that same steadiness in our hearts. We place in Your hands that thing that seems finished, because You are the resurrection and You are the life. May we honor You as King all our lives and give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Is there something in your heart that you have already come to face “carrying spices,” convinced there will be no turning point? What has God’s word said about it?
2\. If you looked at the most recent scene that threw you into panic from an eternal viewpoint, how would you reinterpret it?

v: But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. So as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
They asked her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”
Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ ”
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.
b: This is the first encounter on Resurrection morning.
Not in the temple.
Not in the synagogue.
It was outside a tomb.
The first words the Lord spoke after He rose
were not a proclamation,
not a teaching,
but a name:
“Mary.”
The whole Gospel of John has come to this point,
from the water turned to wine in Galilee,
all the way to the empty tomb in Jerusalem.
And the first light of the resurrection
fell on a woman weeping so hard she could hardly stand.
1. The disciples went home, but she stayed outside the tomb
Verse 11 begins with one word
that is easy to read past:
“But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping.”
That word “but”
is a contrast.
Verse 10 just before says
that Peter and the other disciple “went away again to their own homes.”
They had looked,
had checked it out,
and then gone home.
Only Mary stayed behind.
She had no answers.
She had no plan.
She had only one thing:
she would not leave.
Dear family,
notice the order here.
It is not that she understood first
and then stayed.
She stayed first,
and then met the Lord.
We often think
that we must wait until it all makes sense in our hearts,
until our questions are resolved,
before we have the right to draw near to God.
But this passage tells us:
staying when it does not yet make sense
is itself a kind of faith.
The one who stayed
met the Lord.
Her tears were not shed in vain.
Her tears
kept her in the very place where the Lord would appear.
2. When sorrow is too full, even angels seem unremarkable
Verse 12 says
that she stooped and looked into the tomb
and “saw two angels in white sitting.”
Two angels.
In white.
One at the head,
one at the feet.
In the whole Bible,
this is an immensely significant vision.
Anyone else
would have fallen on the ground at once.
But what was Mary’s reaction?
The angels asked her:
“Woman, why are you weeping?”
She said:
“Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”
She was not stunned by the angels at all.
She simply went on answering the one thing in her heart.
Why?
Because her heart was already full.
So full
that even the greatest miracle could not squeeze in.
In the depths of grief,
the eyes are clouded with tears.
It is not that she was unspiritual.
It is how people truly are.
We have had days like that ourselves.
The day the diagnosis came into our hands.
The night a loved one passed away.
After the phone call that told us something had happened to our child.
In those days
we still read the Word,
still gathered,
but could take nothing in.
The Lord knows.
The Lord did not rebuke her:
“How can you see angels and not worship?”
The Lord did not say:
“Your faith is too small.”
The Lord simply,
quietly,
came to stand behind her.
3. The Lord was standing beside her all along, only we do not recognize Him
Verse 14
is the most moving sentence in the whole passage:
“When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, and didn’t know that it was Jesus.”
She saw Him,
yet did not know.
The Lord had been standing there all along.
He did not come after she had wept enough.
He did not come after her faith was great enough.
While she was still weeping,
the Lord was already standing beside her.
Jesus spoke to her:
“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?”
The first words of the risen Lord
were a question.
It was not that He did not know the answer.
He wanted her to say what was in her heart.
And how did Mary answer?
Verse 15:
“She, supposing him to be the gardener,”
She supposed the Lord was the gardener.
She even said:
“tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
She wanted to carry the Lord’s body away with her own hands.
One woman
carrying the body of a grown man.
That was impossible.
But that is how love is.
Love says things that cannot be done.
Dear family,
this scene tells us something very important:
when we weep,
the Lord is often right beside us.
It is just that we do not recognize Him.
We think He is “the gardener.”
We think it is only a stranger,
a phone call that came suddenly,
a casual greeting from someone,
a passage of Scripture we happened to turn to.
In fact it was the Lord standing beside us all along.
The 321 principles say:
the focus is on Jesus,
not on self,
not on others,
not on circumstances.
When our focus is locked only on “where is the body,”
we cannot see the living Lord.
When our eyes are fixed only on the one thing we have lost,
we cannot recognize the One who is speaking to us.
4. He called her by name
Verse 16,
the turning point is only two words:
“Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’”
He did not first explain the doctrine of the resurrection.
He did not first rebuke her slowness.
He did not first prove who He was.
He simply called her name.
The moment that call came out,
Mary immediately turned
and cried out in Hebrew:
“Rabboni!”
which means “Teacher.”
One second before, she could not recognize Him.
This second, she recognized Him.
In between, there was no sermon,
no theology,
only a name.
I think of a scene.
In a very noisy hall,
announcements keep playing,
voices,
footsteps,
the wheels of suitcases,
and you are not really listening to anything.
But the moment the announcement reads your name,
you lift your head at once.
Strange, isn’t it?
The volume did not get louder.
The surroundings did not get quieter.
What changed was—
that voice was calling “me.”
Jesus said in John 10:3
that the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.”
Isaiah 43:1 says:
“I have called you by your name. You are mine.”
Dear family,
\*\*the deepest moment of knowing God is often not that I came to know Him, but that I discovered He knows me.\*\*
It is not that I finally figured God out.
It is that I discovered
He has always known my name.
Knows where I live.
Knows what I have been weeping about these days.
Mary’s faith was not restored by reasoning.
It was restored by being called.
5. “Do not hold on to me”: from clinging to Him, to being sent out by Him
Verse 17,
the Lord said a sentence often misunderstood:
“Don’t touch me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father.”
In the original, this sentence
is not “don’t touch me,”
but “don’t keep clinging to me.”
Because later Thomas touched the Lord’s hands,
and the Lord Himself invited him to touch.
So this is not a refusal.
It is an explanation:
the relationship is about to change.
Before, she could hold the Lord with her hands.
From now on,
the Lord would live in her through the Holy Spirit.
From bodily presence
to a deeper, wider presence.
From one place
to every place.
From her alone
to all who believe in Him.
Here is a little picture.
A person holds a handful of water in the palm of the hand.
The water is real.
But however tightly it is held,
it is only enough to moisten one’s own lips,
and it soon leaks away through the fingers.
But if that water is let into the pipes,
it can reach the kitchen,
reach the bathroom,
reach the whole street.
When the Lord said “do not hold on to me,”
He was not taking the water out of her hands.
He was connecting the water to the pipeline
so that the whole household could drink.
She could not keep the Lord,
but she could be sent out by the Lord.
Then the Lord said a startling thing:
“go to my brothers.”
My brothers.
Who were those people?
They were the ones who days before had sworn never to leave Him
and then all ran away.
They included Peter, who denied the Lord three times.
The Lord did not call them “those disciples,”
did not call them “those failures.”
The Lord called them—
my brothers.
Hebrews 2:11 says:
“he is not ashamed to call them brothers.”
Then the Lord said:
“I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”
Listen to these words:
my Father,
and your Father.
Before the cross,
no one dared speak like that.
After the cross,
the Lord’s Father became our Father.
Romans 8:15 says
that what we received
is “the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’”
Our relationship with the Lord
was completely changed from then on.
The Light of the 321 Principles—Life first, then relationship, then ministry
Today’s passage
plays out step by step the road of “life first, relationship second, ministry last.”
The first step is life.
The Lord called her name.
“Mary.”
Her dead heart
came alive in that one call.
The Lord did not first assign her work.
The Lord first brought her very self back.
The second step is relationship.
“my Father and your Father, my God and your God.”
The Lord first made the relationship clear.
First brothers,
first children,
first family.
The third step is ministry.
“Go to my brothers, and tell them…”
Verse 18,
and she really went:
“I have seen the Lord!”
She became the first to report the resurrection.
In that age,
a woman’s testimony was not even admitted in court.
Yet the Lord gave the greatest good news in human history
first to the most grief-stricken weeper.
Dear family,
notice that this order cannot be reversed.
Without the call of the first step,
the third step is only drudgery.
Many ministries grow weary,
grow bitter,
get done until the heart is dry,
and the reason is often right here:
we are pushed along by responsibility,
not called out by the Lord.
Those pushed along by responsibility
think in their hearts:
“Who is going to do this?”
“Why is it always me?”
“How long do I have to hold on?”
Those called out by the Lord
think in their hearts:
“I have seen the Lord.”
“I cannot but speak.”
\*\*The starting point of ministry is not need but a calling; not being pushed out by people, but being called out by the Lord.\*\*
A person who knows she has been called by name by the Lord
will go far.
Because she is not going to complete a task.
She is going to tell of something she saw with her own eyes.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, the one who stayed met the Lord. It is not that we understand first and then stay; we stay first and then see.
Second, the Lord does not rebuke our weakness. He knows that in grief a person can see nothing, and He still stands beside us.
Third, when we weep, the Lord is often at our side. We just so often take Him for “the gardener.”
Fourth, the deepest moment of knowing God is discovering that He knows me. He can call my name, and He knows what I am weeping about.
Fifth, the starting point of ministry is being called by the Lord, not pushed by responsibility. Life first, then relationship, then ministry; the order cannot be reversed.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that on that morning, the first words the risen Lord spoke were a person’s name. Lord, within us too there is a morning outside the tomb: there are losses we cannot yet walk out of, and tears we have not told anyone. As on that day, stand beside us, call our names, and let us recognize that You are right here. Forgive us for so often staring only at the one thing we have lost and treating You as a stranger, “the gardener”; cleanse our eyes so that our focus is on Jesus alone. Thank You for calling us brothers, so that Your Father becomes our Father and Your God becomes our God. Heal our life first, then mend our relationships, and then send us out. May our ministry not be pushed along by responsibility, but be because we have truly seen the Lord and cannot but speak. Use us, and give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
