v: When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle, and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord.
Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”
When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!
If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”
b: This was the evening of the resurrection day.
In the morning,
Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.
During the day,
Peter and John ran to the tomb to look,
and then went back to their own homes.
By evening,
this little group was hiding in a room.
The doors
were shut.
Jesus came into just such a room
and appeared to the disciples together for the first time.
In just five short verses,
we find peace,
wounds,
a sending,
the Holy Spirit,
and the commission of the gospel.
The church
began on this very night.
I. People can shut the door, but they cannot shut out the Lord
Verse 19 is very specific:
“where the disciples were, for fear of the Jews, the doors being locked.”
Why shut the doors?
Because of fear.
Their teacher had been crucified.
They themselves had scattered and run.
If the religious leaders made a move,
they would be next.
So they shut the doors.
This is the most natural human reaction when afraid:
shut the door.
Avoid people.
Don’t go out.
Hide yourself away.
The original wording means the doors were locked,
bolted.
Not casually pulled closed,
but deliberately sealed.
And then the passage says:
“Jesus came and stood in the middle.”
The door had not opened.
Yet the Lord was inside.
They used doors to keep people out,
but the Lord does not need a door.
Dear family,
please hear this one sentence clearly:
\*\*People can shut the door, but they cannot shut out the Lord.\*\*
There are many closed doors in our lives too.
Some doors were closed after someone hurt us.
Some doors were closed after too many disappointments.
Some doors we closed ourselves,
because we felt too ashamed to face anyone, and so we locked ourselves in.
We often say to others:
I’m fine.
I don’t need anything.
I can manage on my own.
Those are all words of a closed door.
Today there may be someone in our family
whose heart is tightly shut,
who thinks no one can get in
and doesn’t want anyone to.
I want to tell you:
the risen Lord can still stand in the middle.
He does not break the door down.
He does not force you to open it.
He stands among you,
the One who speaks first.
II. At the very moment they deserved rebuke, the Lord said, “Peace be to you”
After the Lord came in,
what was His first sentence?
“Peace be to you!”
Let us think:
if it had been us,
what would our first words have been?
That night,
one had denied Him three times.
Some had fallen asleep in the garden of Gethsemane.
Everyone had run away.
At the foot of the cross stood
only a few women and one John.
He had every right to ask:
Why did you run away that night?
He had every right to say:
I told you so.
But He did not.
He said:
“Peace be to you.”
In Hebrew this word is “shalom.”
It is not only “don’t be afraid,”
but “everything is whole,
complete,
reconciled.”
The Lord meant:
between us,
there is no account left to settle.
That debt
I have already paid in full on the cross.
\*\*At the very moment rebuke was due, the Lord gave peace.\*\*
This is the gospel.
The gospel is not “first fix yourself, then I will accept you.”
The gospel is “I accept you first, and then you can be changed.”
Dear family,
if today you feel in your heart:
in my condition,
the Lord must be so disappointed.
I fell so badly this time,
He probably doesn’t want anything to do with me anymore.
please come back to this verse.
The first words He spoke when He came in
were not an accounting.
They were peace.
III. The wounds were not erased—the wounds became the proof
Verse 20,
“When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side.”
This is a wonderful thing.
Jesus’ body had already been raised.
He could pass through locked doors.
He had already conquered death.
By all reason,
such a glorious body
should bear no more wounds.
Yet His hands still had the nail marks.
His side still had the opening from the spear.
Later, when Thomas came,
the Lord even said to him,
“Reach here your finger, and see my hands; and reach here your hand, and put it into my side.”
The risen Lord
is a Lord who bears scars.
Why?
Because those scars are the proof.
The proof that “I truly died for you.”
The proof that “I am truly the One.”
The moment the disciples saw those hands,
they knew Him.
The passage says:
“Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.”
Their joy
came from the wounds.
I think of a way of mending porcelain.
A bowl has been smashed,
and someone refuses to throw it away.
They glue the pieces back together with lacquer,
and then trace every crack with gold dust.
Once it is mended,
the cracks are not hidden;
instead they are traced out clearly.
And the most beautiful part of that bowl
is the very place where it was broken.
Dear family,
God does not necessarily remove the scars from us.
Some wounds
He heals,
yet a mark remains.
Some things
He restores,
yet He does not make you forget.
But please believe:
He can turn that scar into a testimony.
A person who has never hurt
cannot comfort those who hurt.
A person who has never fallen
cannot lift up those who have fallen.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“by his wounds we are healed.”
The Lord uses His wounds
to heal our wounds.
And then He uses our healed wounds
to touch other people’s wounds.
IV. “As the Father has sent me, even so I send you”
Verse 21,
the Lord said again:
“Peace be to you!”
And then went on:
“As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”
Notice the words “even so.”
The Lord does not send us out casually.
He sends us “in the same way the Father sent Him.”
How did the Father send Him?
He was in the form of God,
yet He humbled Himself
and became like a man.
He did not stand at a distance and shout.
He entered into the midst of people.
He ate with tax collectors.
He touched lepers.
He washed the disciples’ feet.
In the end He gave His life for sinners.
That is the way of being sent.
So
the church is not a shelter.
The church is a people who are sent out.
Though the doors were shut,
the Lord came in
not to hide with them,
but to send them out.
And this
cannot be done by human strength.
So verse 22 follows immediately:
“When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit!’”
The very next word after the sending
is the Holy Spirit.
This is no coincidence.
Without the Holy Spirit,
being sent is just toil.
Without the Holy Spirit,
serving is just activity.
This act of “breathing on them”
appears only a few times in the whole Bible.
The most important is
Genesis 2:7:
“Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.”
The first man
came alive because God breathed on him.
The new man
also comes alive because the Lord breathed on him.
2 Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.”
The new creation
begins with this breath.
Dear family,
the power of our service
does not come from ourselves.
It does not come from eloquence.
It does not come from gifts,
experience,
or methods.
It comes from that breath.
V. “Whoever’s sins you forgive”—this is a commission, not an authority
Verse 23 is the verse in this passage most easily misunderstood:
“Whoever’s sins you forgive, they are forgiven them. Whoever’s sins you retain, they have been retained.”
This verse must be explained clearly.
It does not mean the disciples now had the authority to forgive sins.
The authority to forgive sins
has always belonged to God alone.
The Bible is very clear:
only God can forgive sins.
So what did the Lord mean?
He meant:
the church, in the Lord’s name,
proclaims the gospel that has already been accomplished.
When people hear it
and receive it,
their sins are forgiven.
When people hear it
and reject it,
their sins remain.
Forgiveness is not issued by the disciples;
it is proclaimed by the disciples.
I think of a mail carrier delivering a letter.
There is a letter
that says the debt has been paid in full.
The mail carrier did not write the letter.
The carrier has no authority to change a single word on it.
Nor can the carrier decide whom to forgive.
But once the letter is delivered
and the person opens it and reads it,
his debt is truly cleared.
If the letter stays in the mailbag,
undelivered,
that person goes on carrying the debt,
day after day.
We are that mail carrier.
The Lord wrote the letter.
The Lord paid the price.
We are only responsible to deliver it.
So what the Lord says next
is not a privilege;
it is an extremely solemn commission.
Because the letter in our hands
concerns a person’s eternity.
Light from the 321 principles—the Holy Spirit is my guide
The third of the three foundations says:
The Holy Spirit is my guide.
Today’s passage
makes this point as clearly as it can be made.
The Lord first said:
I send you.
Then the Lord immediately said:
Receive the Holy Spirit.
The order cannot be reversed.
If there is only the sending
and no Holy Spirit,
we will do many things
but bear no fruit.
We will be very busy
and not know what we are busy with.
We will use our heads to plan,
to analyze,
to compare,
to prop things up,
and in the end be left with nothing but weariness.
The 321 principles say:
Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use the head and rely on yourself.
Using the head brings worry;
using the heart brings joy.
The disciples, behind shut doors,
were using their heads to calculate:
how dangerous it is outside,
how long we can hide.
When the Lord breathed on them,
He reconnected their hearts to the source of life.
Later, this group who hid behind the doors
stood in the main streets of Jerusalem and preached boldly.
It was not because the situation had become safe.
The situation had not changed.
It was because Someone more was inside them.
And the first thing the Holy Spirit does when He comes in
is let Jesus be King.
Not let us be king,
not let my opinion,
my methods,
my pride be king.
It is to let Jesus
in us,
in the midst of the church,
in our service,
truly sit on the throne.
When Jesus is King,
no door can hold us in.
Our Response to Life
This passage reminds us:
First, people can shut the door, but they cannot shut out the Lord. No matter how long your heart’s door has been shut, the risen Lord can still stand in the middle.
Second, the Lord’s first word was not rebuke but peace. He does not bring up old accounts first, because He has already paid that account in full on the cross.
Third, God does not necessarily remove our scars; He makes the scar a testimony. A wound that has been healed can reach out and touch another’s wound.
Fourth, we are sent in the same way as the Lord—humbling ourselves, entering into the midst of people, giving ourselves up. The church is not a shelter; it is a people who are sent out.
Fifth, the power for service does not come from ourselves; it comes from that breath. Without the Holy Spirit, being sent is just toil; with the Holy Spirit, even the weak can stand in the street.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your Son Jesus Christ, who on that night when every door was shut still stood among His disciples and said, “Peace be to you.” Lord, we confess that we also have many closed doors in our hearts—some closed because people hurt us, some closed because we are ashamed. Come into us today, not to settle accounts, but to give peace. Thank You for showing us Your hands and side, so that we know You truly died for us; and make the scars on our own lives into proof of comfort for others. Lord, You said that as the Father sent You, so You send us; breathe on us, let the Holy Spirit fill us, so that we do not prop things up with our heads and rely on ourselves, but walk with our hearts relying on the Holy Spirit. Reign in us as King, and let us faithfully deliver Your gospel into the hands of those who have not yet heard it, and give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Which door in your heart is shut right now? If the risen Lord stood in the middle of that room today, what would He say to you first?
2\. Is there a scar in you that still hurts, that you don’t want anyone to see? Ask the Lord to show you whether this scar could become comfort to someone.

v: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”
b: The risen Lord had already appeared.
The disciples had seen Him with their own eyes.
But one man was not there.
His name was Thomas.
This passage
is, in the whole Gospel of John,
the one that comes closest to us.
Because for two thousand years,
the great majority of believers
have never seen the Lord with their own eyes.
We all stand where Thomas stood.
And the last sentence the Lord spoke
was spoken to us.
I. He missed Him because he wasn’t there
Verse 24 is stated plainly,
yet it pierces the heart:
“But Thomas was not with them when Jesus came.”
The Bible does not blame Thomas.
It simply records, very honestly, a fact:
that day,
he was not there.
When the Lord came,
the doors were shut,
the people were afraid,
their faith was low.
The conditions were just as bad.
But those who stayed saw the Lord.
Thomas did not.
The reason he missed Him is simple.
It was not that he was less spiritual.
It was not that he loved the Lord less.
It was only that—
he wasn’t there.
We often assume
that missing what God is doing must be because of some great failure.
More often,
it is only because of absence.
And why do people become absent?
What Thomas was thinking in those days
the Bible does not say.
But we can imagine.
He had watched the Lord be crucified.
He had staked his whole life’s hope on Him.
And the hope was shattered at the cross.
A heartbroken person
what he least wants to see
is people.
He wanted to be alone for a while.
He wanted to withdraw from the group
and digest the pain by himself.
That is human nature.
But it was this very human nature
that made him miss the Lord.
Dear family,
this is a very practical reminder for today:
when we are hurting,
we are most likely to withdraw from the group.
When we withdraw from the group,
we are most likely to miss the Lord.
\*\*Do not leave your brothers and sisters at the moment you are weakest.\*\*
That is exactly when you most need to stay among them.
Hebrews 10:25 says:
“not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is.”
In a jigsaw puzzle,
if one piece is missing,
the whole picture is still on the wall,
and you can still make out the image.
The one who really loses out is that piece.
It lies in a corner,
cut off from the whole picture,
seeing nothing,
not even knowing where it belongs.
II. Thomas was not a bad man—he was the one who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him”
We often stick a label on Thomas:
Doubting Thomas.
That is actually very unfair to him.
Thomas appears three times in John’s Gospel.
The first time
was when Lazarus died.
Everyone was urging Jesus not to go to Judea,
because the people there wanted to stone Him.
Only Thomas said:
“Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
What courage that was.
The second time
was at the Last Supper.
Jesus said He was going to prepare a place for them.
Thomas said honestly:
“Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
(John 14:5)
He did not pretend to understand.
He did not just nod along.
When he had a question in his heart,
he said it out loud.
The third time
is today’s passage.
So what kind of man was Thomas?
He was a man of deep feeling.
He was an honest man.
He was also a man who must have solid evidence.
He loved deeply,
so he fell hard.
He would not brush things aside with a quick “I believe,”
because he was unwilling to hold on to a false hope once again.
Brothers and sisters,
doubt is not the same as unbelief.
Doubt is often a sign that you still care.
True unbelief
is no longer even wanting to ask,
turning away
and never coming back.
Thomas was still asking,
which shows he was still on the inside.
But there was one problem with Thomas:
he wanted to confirm it with his own hands.
“Unless I see… and put my finger into… and put my hand into… I will not believe.”
Three verbs,
all with “I.”
I see.
I put in.
I confirm.
He held the control of faith
in his own hands.
This is the deepest kind of “self.”
It is not that he did not believe in God,
but that he wanted God to prove Himself to him in his own way.
III. For the sake of one person, the Lord came again
Verse 26:
“After eight days again his disciples were inside, and Thomas with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked.”
Eight days.
Thomas carried his doubts
through a full eight days.
Those eight days must have been hard.
His companions told him daily that they had seen the Lord,
and he alone had not.
But notice one thing:
though he doubted,
he still returned to the disciples.
He did not stop coming
just because he couldn’t say “I believe.”
That one step
saved him.
And then
the Lord came.
The first time Jesus appeared
was for that whole group.
This time He appeared
for that one person.
A play is not restarted from the beginning
because one audience member arrived late.
A train does not back up to the platform
because one passenger missed it.
But our Lord does.
For the sake of one who was still doubting,
He passed through locked doors
and came again.
And what He said is even more startling:
“Reach here your finger, and see my hands; and reach here your hand, and put it into my side.”
Please take this sentence,
and what Thomas said in verse 25,
and set them side by side.
Not a word differs.
Thomas said, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands,”
and the Lord said, “See my hands.”
Thomas said, “and put my hand into His side,”
and the Lord said, “put it into my side.”
In that moment Thomas understood:
every word I spoke during those eight days outside,
the Lord heard.
He was not in front of me,
yet He was listening all along.
The Lord is not afraid of our questions.
\*\*What He fears is that we carry our questions and refuse to come to Him.\*\*
Questions brought to the Lord
become the doorway to faith.
Questions hidden in the heart and left unspoken
ferment into bitterness and coldness.
So the Lord finally said:
“Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
The tone in the original is:
Do not stay stuck in a state of unbelief;
become a believing person.
The Lord was not rebuking him.
The Lord was lending him a hand,
pulling him from outside the door to inside.
IV. “My Lord and my God!”—the highest confession in the whole book
Verse 28,
Thomas said:
“My Lord and my God!”
These few words
are the highest peak of faith’s confession in the whole Gospel of John.
At the very start, John’s Gospel says:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
(John 1:1)
Having come this far,
the beginning and the end meet.
At the opening of the book,
the Holy Spirit declared through John’s pen: the Word was God.
Before the book closes,
a man who once doubted
kneels before the risen Lord and says with his own mouth:
My Lord and my God.
From the declaration of truth
to personal surrender.
This is the road John’s Gospel means to walk us through to the end.
And notice two words:
My.
Not “He is Lord.”
But “my Lord.”
Not “God exists.”
But “my God.”
When faith moves from “He is” to “my,”
that is what it means to be saved.
And there is one more thing
that many readers pass over:
from beginning to end, the text
never records that Thomas actually reached out and touched Him.
The Lord permitted him to touch.
But he did not touch.
Because when the Lord stood before him
and spoke aloud the very words hidden in his heart,
he no longer needed to touch.
The evidence
became unnecessary at the moment he met the Lord.
We often ask God for a sign,
a confirmation,
some visible proof.
But those who truly meet the Lord find
that when He comes,
the very things we wanted
fall away by themselves.
V. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe
Verse 29,
Jesus said:
“Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”
This sentence is wonderful.
Because everyone in that room
believed after seeing.
So to whom is the Lord’s blessing spoken?
It is spoken to those not yet born.
It is spoken to every reader of this book
over two thousand years.
It is spoken to you and me,
sitting here this morning in devotion.
The Lord’s eyes passed beyond that room
and saw us.
1 Peter 1:8 says:
“whom, not having seen, you love. In him, though now you don’t see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy unspeakable and full of glory.”
This is us.
We have not seen,
yet we love Him.
We cannot see Him,
yet we have great joy.
Hebrews 11:1 says:
“Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.”
Faith is not shutting your eyes and guessing.
Faith is relying on the word of God
and standing on what has not yet been seen.
So in verse 31 John goes on to state his purpose in writing this book:
“but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing you may have life in his name.”
What Thomas gained with his finger,
we gain by faith.
And the Lord says:
such people
are blessed.
Light from the 321 principles—use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use the head and rely on yourself
Thomas’s problem
was not that he did not love the Lord enough.
It was that he wanted to use his head,
his eyes,
his finger
to confirm a spiritual matter.
The 321 principles keep reminding us:
use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit;
don’t use the head and rely on yourself.
Using the heart brings joy;
using the head brings worry.
Those eight days,
was Thomas happy?
Not at all.
He analyzed over and over,
turned it over and over,
asked himself again and again:
could they have been mistaken?
Could it have been a hallucination?
If it was real, why was I the one who wasn’t there?
The faster the mind turned,
the bitterer the heart became.
Because the head is for handling matters,
not for holding God.
The organ God placed in us to know Him
is the heart.
The effects of a whole life
flow out from the heart.
We can also look at this passage through the “eight steps of changing a mindset.”
The first three of the eight steps are:
information,
revelation,
conviction.
The disciples said to Thomas:
“We have seen the Lord.”
That is information.
The information was true.
The information was also precious.
But information cannot change a person’s life.
Thomas heard information for a full eight days,
and his heart was still hard.
Until the Lord Himself stood before him—
that is revelation.
Once revelation came,
eight days of arguing were no longer needed, not one sentence of it.
He fell down at once:
My Lord and my God.
That is conviction.
Dear family,
the difference here is very important.
Other people’s testimony
is information.
Meeting the Lord personally
is revelation.
It is like a dish.
Others can tell you about it,
as carefully
and vividly as they like,
and you still won’t know how it tastes.
Only when you take a bite yourself
do you really know.
Psalm 34:8 says:
“Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good.”
It does not say, “Listen to how good Yahweh is.”
It says taste.
So when we have devotions each day,
we do not come to collect more spiritual information.
We come to meet the Lord.
We come so that the Holy Spirit may turn
the word on the page into living revelation within us.
And once revelation comes,
conviction follows.
Our Response to Life
This passage reminds us:
First, do not leave your brothers and sisters when you are weakest. Thomas missed the Lord, not because he failed, but only because he wasn’t there.
Second, doubt is not the same as unbelief. The Lord will surely come looking for one who is still willing to ask, still willing to return among his brothers and sisters.
Third, the Lord will come again for one person. He remembers every word we spoke outside the door.
Fourth, at the moment of meeting the Lord, the evidence becomes unnecessary. What we truly need is not confirmation, but Him.
Fifth, blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe. This blessing the Lord has especially kept for us today.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your Son Jesus Christ, who for the sake of one still-doubting disciple passed through locked doors and came again. Lord, there is a Thomas inside us too—we have also withdrawn from the group because of heartbreak, been absent because of disappointment, and dared not hope again because we could not see. Forgive us, lend us a hand, and pull us from outside the door to inside. Help us no longer to use the head and rely on ourselves, but to use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; no longer to demand that You prove Yourself in our way, but to surrender quietly before You. May Your Spirit turn every word we read from information into revelation, bring us from revelation into conviction, and from conviction into a life lived out. Today we also want to fall down before You as Thomas did and say: You are my Lord, You are my God. Though we have not seen, may we love You with all our hearts, and believing in You, rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory, giving all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Has something recently made you want to “be alone for a while,” and so you left your brothers and sisters? The Lord invites you today to come back inside the door—what step are you willing to take?

2\. Which part of your faith is still stuck at “information”—heard, known, agreed with, yet not yet become the “revelation” of meeting the Lord personally? For what matter will you ask the Lord today to reveal Himself to you personally?

v: Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
b: Today’s passage is only two verses.
Very few words.
Yet extremely weighty.
Because these two verses
are John himself telling us why he wrote this book.
At the very end of a book,
the author suddenly puts down his pen,
turns around, and speaks to the reader:
Why did I write all this?
What do I want you to receive?
From chapter one, “In the beginning was the Word,”
all the way through to the empty tomb,
to Thomas falling down and saying, “My Lord and my God,”
here at the end,
John places the key to the whole book in our hands.
Today let us receive this key together.
I. What was not written down is more than what was
In verse 30,
John says:
“Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book.”
This is a very honest statement.
John admits:
I have not written it all down.
What I wrote
is only a very small part.
In Jesus’ three and a half years of ministry,
how many did He heal?
How many demons did He cast out?
How many words did He speak?
No one can count.
At the very end of this book John also says:
if every one of them were written,
I suppose that even the world itself would not have room for the books that would be written.
So
why didn’t John write more?
It was not for lack of material.
It was because he made choices.
Brothers and sisters,
the Bible is not a running log.
The Bible is not a record of Jesus’ itinerary.
The Bible is a testimony with a purpose.
Here is a picture from everyday life.
A family goes on a ten-day trip,
and comes home with three thousand photos on a phone.
But Mom sits down
and picks through them one by one,
and in the end chooses only thirty,
prints them,
and pastes them into an album.
The two thousand nine hundred seventy photos that were set aside
were not fake photos,
nor bad photos.
They simply could not tell the story.
And the thirty that were kept,
put together,
let a child who opens the album many years later
see again that year,
how Mom and Dad loved him.
What John did
was exactly this.
He did not want us to know every single thing Jesus did.
He wanted us to know who Jesus is.
So he picked.
He chose.
He put in, one by one,
the few events that most clearly reveal the Lord’s identity.
This also reminds us of something:
when we read the Bible,
we often ask:
Why isn’t this written here?
What happened to that matter afterward?
What was that person’s final outcome?
The Bible often does not answer.
Because the Bible was never written to satisfy our curiosity.
The Bible was written so that we would know God,
trust God,
and obey God.
The 321 principles say:
The Bible is my standard.
A standard means:
it is not a database;
it is a measuring rod.
We do not use the Bible to look up information;
we place ourselves before the Bible
and let it measure us.
II. Seven signs, seven doors, leading to the same Lord
What did John choose?
In John’s Gospel
he records only seven miracles in all.
And he does not call them merely “miracles”;
he often uses one word:
“signs.”
The purpose of a sign is not for people to look at the sign,
but for people to follow the sign
and see the One it points to.
Let us review these seven together.
First, turning water into wine at the wedding in Cana.
It says:
the Lord can take the situations in life that have come to an end,
where there is no hope left,
and make them better than before.
Second, healing the official’s son.
The moment the Lord’s word was spoken,
the child far away in Capernaum was well.
It says:
the Lord’s authority is not limited by distance;
however far away the person you care about may be,
the Lord’s word reaches them.
Third, beside the pool of Bethesda,
the man who had lain there for thirty-eight years.
No one put him into the water.
Yet the Lord said to him directly:
Arise, take up your mat, and walk.
It says:
the Lord does not need the pool;
the Lord Himself is the healing.
Fourth, five loaves and two fish feeding five thousand.
It says:
the Lord is the bread of life;
He can take the little that is in your hand
and feed the need you thought could not be fed.
Fifth, walking on the sea.
The wind and waves were raging,
the disciples were straining at the oars,
and the Lord came walking over the very waters they feared.
It says:
what makes you afraid
is only a road under the Lord’s feet.
Sixth, healing the man born blind.
It says:
the Lord is the light of the world;
He does not merely show you the light,
He gives you eyes.
Seventh, raising Lazarus, who had been dead four days.
It says:
the Lord’s authority does not stop at sickness,
nor at hardship,
but all the way to death;
He is Lord throughout.
Seven signs,
seven doors.
Each time a door is pushed open,
the One standing inside is the same.
And each miracle
is paired with an “I am.”
I am the bread of life.
I am the light of the world.
I am the door of the sheep.
I am the good shepherd.
I am the resurrection and the life.
I am the way, the truth, and the life.
I am the true vine.
Family,
please notice one thing.
These seven “I am” statements
are not seven abstract theological terms.
They answer seven real longings in the human heart.
There is a hunger in the human heart,
and the Lord says: I am the bread of life.
There is a darkness in the human heart,
and the Lord says: I am the light of the world.
There is an insecurity in the human heart,
not knowing where I belong,
and the Lord says: I am the door of the sheep.
There is a loneliness in the human heart,
no one truly takes care of me,
and the Lord says: I am the good shepherd.
There is a fear of death in the human heart,
and the Lord says: I am the resurrection and the life.
There is a feeling of being lost in the human heart,
not knowing where life is headed,
and the Lord says: I am the way, the truth, and the life.
There is a dryness in the human heart,
wanting so much to bear fruit but unable to,
and the Lord says: I am the true vine.
So John’s Gospel is not a cold book of doctrine.
It is a shepherd,
speaking sentence by sentence to the deepest gap in your heart:
I am the one.
III. Believing has an object and has content
In verse 31,
John states his purpose:
“but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.”
Notice,
the “believing” here is not empty.
It is not “you must have faith.”
It is not “think positively.”
It is not “if your heart is sincere, it works.”
John is very specific:
believe in “Jesus”—there is a name.
Believe that He “is the Christ”—there is an identity.
Believe that He “is the Son of God”—there is a nature.
Today many people speak of faith
in very hazy terms.
“I believe there is a Ruler over all, too.”
“I think it’s enough to have love in your heart.”
“All religions just teach people to do good.”
These words sound tolerant,
but they are actually very empty.
Because if faith has no object,
faith is only an emotion;
if faith has no content,
faith is only self-comfort.
Here is a picture we all know.
At a wedding,
the groom stands at the front,
and when the pastor asks him,
he does not say:
“I am willing to love all the women in the world.”
He does not say:
“I have a very positive attitude toward marriage.”
He says a name.
A specific name,
spoken by name,
a name he will be responsible for to the very end.
It is because he speaks that name
that the vow carries weight.
Believing in the Lord is the same.
Faith is not a vague religious feeling.
Faith is by name.
It is that I know Him,
and He knows me.
So then,
what does “Christ” mean?
In Hebrew it is “Messiah,”
in Greek it is translated “Christ,”
meaning “the Anointed One.”
In the Old Testament,
three kinds of people were anointed:
prophets,
priests,
and kings.
The prophet brings God’s word to the people.
The priest brings the people before God.
The king governs and protects God’s people.
For hundreds of years Israel waited
for this Anointed One.
And Jesus came.
He is the prophet—
He is the Word made flesh,
the very word of God.
He is the priest—
He did not lead a lamb to offer;
He offered Himself.
He is the king—
only His kingdom is not of this world;
His throne is first set up in the human heart.
Next,
what does “Son of God” mean?
In Jewish ears,
this phrase is very weighty.
It does not mean “God likes Him very much,”
nor “He is a very spiritual man.”
“Son of God” means:
He is of the same nature as the Father,
of the same honor,
of the same glory.
He came out from the Father,
and He and the Father are one.
So when Peter said:
“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
that was not a compliment;
it was a revelation.
Family,
the One we believe in today
is this One.
Not a good man.
Not a moral teacher.
Not a great figure of history.
He is the anointed King,
the Son of God, equal in honor with the Father.
Our faith has an object,
our faith has content,
and so our faith stands firm.
IV. Life in His name—not receiving a religion, but receiving life
The second half of verse 31:
“and that believing you may have life in his name.”
Notice,
John did not say:
believe in Him and you can receive a set of teachings.
He did not say:
believe in Him and you can join a religion.
He did not say:
believe in Him and you can receive a list of rules
and from now on strive to keep them well.
He said:
receive life.
This is the greatest difference between the gospel and religion.
Religion gives you a set of requirements
and tells you to reach them by yourself.
The gospel puts a new life inside you
and lets Christ live out through you.
Religion presses from the outside in.
The gospel flows from the inside out.
Religion deals with behavior.
The gospel deals with life.
The Lord Himself said:
“I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”
And look at these words:
“in His name.”
Not by my effort.
Not by my qualifications.
Not because I am good enough,
devout enough,
useful enough.
It is in His name.
What a comfort this is.
Because if it were in my name,
I would have it today when my devotions stir me,
and lose it tomorrow when my heart goes cold;
I would be sure this month when things go smoothly,
and have no hope next month when I stumble.
But since it is in His name,
my roots are not in me;
they are in Him.
But family,
we need to take one more step.
Receiving life
is not the finish line;
it is the starting line.
When a child is born,
the hospital gives a birth certificate.
That paper is very important;
it proves that the child has truly come into the world.
But no parent would frame that paper and hang it on the wall
and say:
There,
it’s finished.
Because after the birth
there is still feeding,
still learning to walk,
still learning to talk,
still growing up,
still the day when he can stand on his own and serve others.
Birth is the beginning of life,
not the whole of life.
Believing in the Lord is the same.
The day we made our decision,
the day we were baptized,
was the birth of a new life.
From that day on,
this life must be lived out.
The 321 principles say it very clearly:
change the mindset, and you change life;
change life, and you change the way you live.
Life first,
then relationships,
then ministry.
From the inside out,
five levels of change:
mindset,
life,
lifestyle,
relationships,
ministry.
First the mindset is turned around—
I no longer look at things with human eyes;
I begin to look with God’s eyes.
Then life is renewed—
that “self” is peeled off layer by layer,
and Christ gradually grows within me.
Then the way I live changes—
my time,
my money,
my words,
my temper,
are touched by the Lord one by one.
Then relationships are restored—
relationships at home,
relationships at work,
relationships in the church
begin to carry the fragrance of Christ.
Only last can we speak of ministry.
Never walk it in reverse.
Walking in reverse
means having ministry without life,
service without relationships,
busyness without Christ.
There is one more thing here worth noticing.
By this point in John’s Gospel,
the purpose has been fully declared.
By all reason,
the book could end.
But the Holy Spirit did not let it stop here.
There is still chapter twenty-one.
And what does chapter twenty-one record?
It is the Lord at the Sea of Tiberias,
building a charcoal fire,
preparing breakfast,
and then asking Peter three times:
“Do you love me more than these?”
It is the story of a failed man being restored.
Brothers and sisters,
this is so beautiful.
The Bible does not stop at the declaration of a doctrine;
the Bible goes on to stop at the restoration of one person.
If truth does not land on a specific person,
truth has not yet gone its last mile.
So,
if today you feel you are that failed man,
feel you are unworthy,
feel the Lord has already crossed you off,
please remember:
after declaring “believe in Him and have life,”
the first thing He did
was go to the seashore to find the man who had denied Him three times,
build a fire for him,
give him breakfast,
and ask him:
Do you love me?
Light from the 321 principles—let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory
Today’s passage
strings the 321 principles together into one line from beginning to end.
Let us walk along it.
Of the three foundations,
the first is right there in verse 30.
Jesus is my example—
the seven signs John selected
are not for us to imitate the miracles,
but for us to know the One,
and then follow the One.
The second is in verse 31.
The Bible is my standard—
John tells us himself:
why I wrote.
The Bible has its own purpose,
and when we read it,
we must read according to its purpose.
The third is in the very breath of the whole book.
The Holy Spirit is my guide—
because these written words,
unless the Holy Spirit opens them,
we read and merely pass over.
It is the Holy Spirit who turns black ink on white paper
into a living word.
With the three foundations in place,
next come the two cores.
After we believe
and receive life,
where do we go from here?
The answer is these two lines:
Let Jesus be King.
Let Jesus receive all the glory.
To let Jesus be King
means:
He is the Christ,
the anointed King,
so His kingship cannot only hang on our lips.
If He is King,
He must be King over my time.
King in my wallet.
King in my home.
King over my anger.
King in that corner that I least want to hand over.
If our mouths confess Him as King
but in our hearts we ourselves sit on the throne,
that is having faith
without having His lordship.
To let Jesus receive all the glory
means:
after I receive life,
this life is not for glorifying myself.
Not for proving that I am spiritual.
Not for comparing who has the bigger gift.
John wrote a whole book
and from beginning to end did only one thing:
keep the focus on Jesus.
He did not even write his own name,
saying only “the disciple whom the Lord loved.”
This is letting Jesus receive the glory.
Finally, there is one purpose:
to build God’s system.
A person believes,
receives life,
lets Jesus be King,
gives the glory to the Lord,
and then what?
Then comes walking with others.
It is the 2 of spiritual companions,
the 3 of spiritual parents and children,
the 5 of spiritual comrades,
built up together
to become God’s family on earth.
So,
dear family,
please remember the most important sentence today:
Believing is not the finish line;
believing is the starting line.
John wrote this book
not so that after reading it we would say:
“So that is what Jesus is like.”
He wrote it so that after reading it
we would kneel down and say:
“Lord, You are my King.”
Our Response to Life
This passage reminds us:
First, the Bible is a testimony with a purpose, not a running log. Every word God has left us is so that we may know Him and trust Him.
Second, the seven signs and seven “I am” statements all point to the same Lord. He is answering the deepest longing in your heart.
Third, believing has an object and has content. What we believe in is Jesus, the Christ, the Son of God—not a vague religious feeling.
Fourth, the result of the gospel is receiving life, not receiving a religion. Life begins with birth, and then must be lived out from the inside out.
Fifth, believing is not the finish line but the starting line. After receiving life comes letting Jesus be King, letting Him receive all the glory, and building God’s system.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we thank You for giving us the Gospel of John. Thank You for Your servant John, who faithfully wrote down what matters most, so that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Lord, we confess that we often leave our faith in knowledge—we have read much, but have not truly handed our lives over to You. Have mercy on us, remove the hazy and empty faith within us, and let us fix our eyes on You clearly: You are the anointed King, You are the Son of God equal in honor with the Father, You are the Lord I will follow all my life. Thank You for giving life, not by my name, but by Your name. Let this life live out from within, changing my mindset, renewing my life, turning my lifestyle around, restoring my relationships, and only then entrusting me with the commission to serve. May Jesus be King in me, may all the glory be Yours, and may You build God’s system through us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself this way.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out, and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing.
But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus.
Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.

That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.
But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish.
b: The Gospel of John has reached its last chapter.
The cross is past.
The tomb is empty.
The Lord has risen
and has already appeared to the disciples.
By all reason,
the story should be over.
But the Holy Spirit moved John
to write this one more chapter.
Because there was one thing not yet finished—
Peter had not yet been restored.
This passage
is the risen Lord at the seashore,
walking step by step toward a disciple who had fallen.
I. “I am going fishing”—a man who has failed goes back to what he knows how to do
In verse 3,
Simon Peter said to them:
“I’m going fishing.”
That sentence is short.
So short it sounds like a passing remark.
But if we remember who Peter was,
we will hear the weight beneath it.
Peter is the one who denied the Lord three times by the fire.
He is the one who beat his chest and said he would die with Him.
He had seen with his own eyes that the Lord had risen,
and the Lord had already appeared to them.
But the wound in his heart
was still there.
Some of our family may ask:
Peter going back to fishing,
was that a step backward?
Was it a fall?
We must speak very carefully.
The Bible here does not rebuke him.
The Lord Himself afterward did not rebuke him for fishing.
But we can see a state of heart—
a man who has failed,
not knowing whether the Lord could still use him,
goes back to the one thing he knows he can do.
Because in that, at least,
he is skilled.
In that, at least,
he will not let people down again.
Dear family,
this kind of feeling
is no stranger to us.
When something goes wrong in ministry,
we quietly retreat into our own expertise.
When we are wounded in a relationship,
we go back to doing the thing that requires no risk.
After we have stumbled,
we often do not leave God;
we hide in a corner of “what I can still manage.”
That corner is not necessarily sinful,
but often the Lord is not in it.
II. Toiling all night, yet catching nothing
The second half of verse 3:
“They went out and entered into the boat. That night they caught nothing.”
Notice these conditions.
Peter was a professional fisherman.
He grew up on the Sea of Galilee.
Going with him were the two sons of Zebedee,
who were also fishermen.
It was a sea they knew well.
Night is, after all, the best time for fishing.
The people were right,
the place was right,
the time was right,
the tools were right.
And the result?
They caught nothing.
Not a single fish.
This was not bad luck.
This was God’s deliberate arrangement.
Because the Lord wanted them to experience one thing personally:
apart from Him,
even the thing we do best cannot be done.
The Lord Himself said in chapter 15:
“For apart from me you can do nothing.”
Psalm 127:1 also says:
“Unless Yahweh builds the house, they labor in vain who build it.”
We often assume
that failure comes from not trying hard enough.
But there is a kind of failure
that comes precisely from relying too much on our own effort.
It is like a man running on a treadmill all night.
Breathing hard,
drenched in sweat,
legs aching,
heart racing.
From the standpoint of effort,
beyond reproach.
But when dawn comes,
he is still in the same place.
Not one step forward.
Because that was not a road;
it was a treadmill.
Sometimes God lets us come away with nothing,
not to shame us.
It is so that before daybreak
we can see one thing clearly:
\*\*I have been straining all along, but not straining in Him.\*\*
III. As day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore
Verse 4,
“But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.”
This verse is beautiful.
First, the time the Lord came.
Not when they were pleased with themselves.
Not when they were returning with a full catch.
It was when they were weary from a whole night,
returning empty-handed.
The Lord often appears “as day is breaking.”
At the moment when the night is longest,
people are most exhausted,
and the nets are emptiest.
Second, the place the Lord came.
Jesus did not wait for them in the temple.
He stood on the shore.
He came to the place where they were toiling.
The Lord did not begin by asking:
“Why did you go back to fishing?”
The first thing He asked was:
“Children, have you any fish?”
The word “children”
in the original is a very tender form of address,
like a father calling his own child.
The Lord used the tone of family,
not the tone of an interrogation.
And what He asked
was a question they could not answer with any pride.
They could only answer honestly:
“No.”
Dear family,
admitting “I have nothing” before the Lord
is the first step of restoration.
Sometimes the reason we are slow to be touched by the Lord
is not that we are too weak,
but that we are still gritting our teeth,
still able to say, “I’m fine,”
“It’s okay,”
“I can handle it myself.”
That night’s empty nets
became their blessing.
Because only an empty hand
can reach out.
IV. “Cast the net on the right side of the boat”—obeying one word is better than a whole night of effort
Verse 6,
Jesus said:
“Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”
“They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.”
Let us compare before and after.
The same sea.
The same net.
The same fishermen.
The tail end of the same night.
Where is the difference?
Only one word.
Only whom they listened to.
All night, they decided where to cast;
at daybreak, the Lord decided where to cast.
When lordship changed hands,
the result was completely different.
It is like a jigsaw puzzle piece.
Sometimes we hold that piece
and press it again and again into the same opening,
pressing until our fingers turn red,
and it will not go in.
It is not that we put it in the wrong place,
nor that a piece is missing.
Just turn it a different direction,
set it down lightly,
and it drops right in.
The same piece,
the same opening,
only the direction was different.
Our lives are often like this.
It is not that we are not exerting enough strength;
it is that we have not handed over the direction.
Interestingly,
this is not the first time Peter has met something like this.
In Luke chapter 5,
on the day they were called,
they had also toiled all night and caught nothing.
Peter said then:
“Master, we worked all night, and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”
The result was a great catch of fish,
and their nets began to break.
The Lord called him
with the same sign,
and now restores him
with the same sign.
How considerate the Lord is.
He knew Peter could not take in a long speech,
so He replayed that lesson from three years ago
exactly as it was.
The moment Peter saw the net full of fish,
his heart understood at once:
It is Him.
V. Putting on his outer garment and jumping into the sea—one who has fallen can still be the first to run to the Lord
Verse 7,
“That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, ‘It’s the Lord!’”
“So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around him (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.”
John recognized Him first;
Peter jumped in first.
John’s eyes were quick;
Peter’s feet were quick.
In the body of the Lord,
He has never wanted only one kind of person.
Here is a very moving detail.
Peter first “put on an outer garment”
and then jumped into the sea.
Ordinarily people take off clothes to jump into water,
but he put them on first.
Because in the Jewish way of thinking,
to meet an honored person
one must not be improperly dressed.
Peter had fallen,
but the reverence in his heart for the Lord was still there.
He did not rush over carelessly;
he rushed over having prepared himself.
And then we see:
Peter is still the same Peter.
Still so impulsive,
still unable to sit still,
still not waiting for the boat to reach shore.
After the resurrection, the Lord
did not replace his temperament.
Only this time,
he rushed in the right direction.
Before, when he rushed,
it was to draw a sword and strike.
Before, when he rushed,
it was to stop the Lord from going to the cross.
This time he rushed
toward the Lord.
Dear family,
please keep this sentence in your heart:
\*\*One who has fallen can still be the first to jump into the water.\*\*
The devil loves to tell those who have failed:
You no longer have a share.
You only deserve to stay at the back.
Just sit quietly.
But this passage tells us:
the man who denied the Lord three times
is here the first one into the water.
The Lord did not put Peter outside the list.
The Lord is calling him back onto the list.
Light from the 321 principles—let Jesus be King: when lordship is in whose hands, the result is completely different
Today’s passage
makes “let Jesus be King” very concrete.
We often think
that letting Jesus be King is a very spiritual, abstract idea.
In fact it is very practical.
So practical it can be measured by one night’s catch.
All night, with ourselves in charge—
the net was empty.
At daybreak, with the Lord in charge—
so many fish that they could not draw it in.
The same men,
the same ability,
the same sea.
Only because lordship changed hands.
So the question was never:
am I strong enough?
The question is:
on this boat,
who is giving the orders?
What the “self” in us is least willing to hand over
is often the decision.
We are willing to work hard for the Lord,
willing to be busy for the Lord,
willing to stay up all night.
We are just not very willing to ask one question:
Lord, which side do You want me to cast on?
The 321 principles also remind us:
use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use the head and rely on yourself.
Using the head brings worry;
using the heart brings joy.
That night, Peter
used only his head.
Where the water is deep,
where the fish are,
which way the wind blows,
how the net should go down.
He used all his experience,
and ended with nothing.
After daybreak,
he did only one thing—
he heard one word
and did as it said.
That catch
was not won by his skill;
it was won by his obedience.
Dear family,
letting Jesus be King
does not mean that after handing over your life you have nothing to do.
The net still has to be cast.
The hands still have to work.
It is only that which side to cast on
is decided by the Lord.
Our Response to Life
This passage reminds us:
First, those who have fallen often hide in a corner they know well. That corner is not necessarily sinful, but often the Lord is not in it.
Second, toiling all night and catching nothing is sometimes God’s grace. He wants us to discover: relying on ourselves, even the thing we do best cannot be done.
Third, the Lord will stand on the shore where we toil, as day is breaking. He does not wait until we triumph to appear; He comes first when we are most weary.
Fourth, obeying one word is better than a whole night of effort. The question is not whether I am strong enough, but who is giving the orders on this boat.
Fifth, one who has fallen can still be the first to run to the Lord. The Lord has not crossed you off; He is calling you back.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that after Your Son Jesus Christ rose, He did not stay in glory waiting for us, but stood on the seashore in the early morning and came to the place where we toil. Lord, we confess that, like Peter, after we stumble we quietly retreat into what we know how to do, using busyness to cover the sense of loss in our hearts. Have mercy on us, and let us dare to say one true word before You: No, this whole night I have nothing. Remove the self within us that refuses to hand over the decision, and let Jesus be King in our hearts, so that we no longer decide by our own experience which side to cast the net on, but use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, listen to Your voice, and do as You say. And heal every one in our family who has failed and feels they no longer have a share; let them run to You again, and become the first to jump into the water. May all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
